#8334. U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

On the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”

“Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”

#8330. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

#8327. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8326. To The Hospital — John Muir Trail Days 7 and 8

After a night in the Motel 6, I got up, took the car keys Sam left me, and went to the Northern Inyo Hospital.  It was a sunny day in Bishop, California.  My stomach was still full of barbecue from the night before.

My hospital! (Photo credit to India M. Clamp)

The people at the hospital were really nice.  They checked me in.  I thought I packed my insurance card but could not find it.  Fortunately, I had my insurance card on my phone and was able to email that to them.  The nurse took my temperature and other vital signs.

A moment later the doctor came in, and I told her about my health, and the John Muir Trail, and how I wondered whether my hike was finished.  Then she put her stethoscope on my chest for about five seconds.  I was puzzled, but she said, “Look, we’re going to take a chest x-ray to rule out pneumonia.  But regardless of the outcome of that x-ray, we’re going to put you on antibiotics.  The x-ray will tell us which particular antibiotic, but that’s about it.”

I agreed (what else was I going to do?) and they wheeled me off for the x-ray.  Then, after the chest x-ray, nothing happened for a long time. I waited in my little cubby in the Emergency Room for about an hour and a half.  I began to wonder what was going on.

In the meantime, I went to the bathroom.  I began to feel cold and asked them for a blanket.  Finally, the doctor returned and said my chest x-ray looked okay.  She said, “We are going to give you Z-pak.”

According to Google AI: “Z-Pak (azithromycin) is a common brand-name prescription antibiotic (Zithromax) taken over a 5-day course to treat bacterial infections like bronchitis, pneumonia, and ear or throat infections.”  Sounded about right.

She said, “Go to Duane’s Pharmacy in town.  You will get six tablets.  Take two today and then one a day for the following four days.”  She also prescribed some codeine cough medication as well as cough pearls.

Then I said, “Well, doctor, you know what my next question is going to be, right?”

She paused for a few seconds and then replied, “You want to know whether you can go back out on the trail.”

I nodded and she said, “I’ll tell you what.  Take off today and take off tomorrow.  See how you respond to the antibiotic.  If you’re feeling a lot better, I think you can go back on the trail.”

Sam and I checked out of the Motel 6 and drove south, stopping for lunch back at the Copper Top BBQ.  We each had the same order:  Tri-Tip hamburgers and chocolate cake.  Oh, it was so good!

Right at that corner in Big Pine was a sign for the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest turnoff.  Having the free time, we drove 45 minutes up into the White Mountains of Inyo County on the east side of the valley (the Sierras are on the west side).  I had never heard of “ancient bristlecone pines” but these trees are apparently the oldest living things on earth.

Bristlecone Pine (thanks to Wal Saravia and Pexels)

Some of these trees are over 4,000 years old.  They live at high altitude in rocky soil under arid conditions.  These factors make them incredibly hardy.  Some are able to continue growing even with just a tiny strip of bark left on them.

Sadly, the location of the oldest tree of all, “Methuselah,” is kept secret to prevent damage from vandals.  Who would do something like that?  But it is not a hypothetical fear.  According to Wikipedia:  “On September 4, 2008, an arsonist set fire to the Schulman Grove Visitor Center and several bristlecone pines. The building and all the exhibits within were destroyed.”  Appalling.

On our way back down, we tried searching for fossils.  We did not have much luck, but we did find a beautiful yellow flowering plant.

Can anyone identify this? Beautiful in any case!

Back in Independence, we checked into the Eastern Sierra Motor Lodge, where we had stayed before setting off the previous week.  It felt like it had been a much longer interval than that.  Sam’s room was for one night; my room was for two nights.

I started to think about unpacking and seeing what I had in the sealed resupply bucket I left in Sam’s car.  No surprise, I had too much food, though not as much as I feared.  The Mount Williamson Motel (of Lauralyn fame) was across the road and had a hiker box for excess food.  So, it would not necessarily go to waste.

That night we went south into Lone Pine and had a steak dinner at Seasons Restaurant.  They ran out of filet mignon, so I had to suffer through a sirloin steak.  What a sacrifice!  I stayed away from the wine for health reasons.  Instead, Sam and I each had a couple of Heineken Zeros.

Sleeping through the night was going to be the big test of the antibiotics.  I had codeine cough medicine and pearls but decided I would not take any – at least at first — because I had taken my two Zithromax at lunch and I wanted to see how I was responding.

Yes, I woke up several times in the night to pee.  But each time I did, I didn’t cough more than two or three times before falling back asleep.  Basically, I slept through the night.

Sam planned to leave for the Las Vegas Airport around mid-morning and asked me to set my alarm so we could go for breakfast together.  When it went off, I immediately asked myself, “How did the night go?”

The answer was promising.  Yes, I felt weak, but I produced much less mucus and coughed much less.  The improvement was dramatic.

Sam and I drove down to Lone Pine to eat at the Alabama Hills Café and Bakery again.  This time we had eggs Benedict with bacon and avocado.  Yes, delicious.  Then we took a drive through the namesake Alabama Hills, famous as the location site for many old Western movies and TV shows.  Many of the boulders are named for images they (ostensibly) suggest and one or two are actually painted.  You can learn more about this area (with pictures) here.

A sample of Alabama Hills (thanks to Allie Feeley and Pexels)

Then we drove back to Independence and soon thereafter, Sam left.  He was headed home.  I was on my own.  Despite my illness, I really enjoyed our time together and appreciated his kindness during my ordeal.  At the same time, I am very used to hiking solo, so there was no anxiety surrounding the change.

After that I loafed about trying to decide how I was feeling, how much impact the antibiotics were having.  I asked myself, “Should I go back on trail tomorrow, or try to take one more day before going back?”  It was a balance between being cautious with my health and being brave enough to get back out there.

I sat outside my room at the motel pondering my options.

The Eastern Sierra Motor Lodge with my socks drying in the foreground and the High Sierra in the background.

Before deciding, I elected to take a walk through town.

First, I dropped off my excess food and gear at the Mount Williamson Motel.  They told me they would not provide transportation to the trailhead for non-guests, but they gave me a name and number for “Mark.”   They said hikers often hired him for that purpose.

I continued down the road, past a stand selling “miel” (honey), and I fell. My first fall on the trail!  It was kind of weird.

The town’s configuration at street crossings entails bright yellow indicators painted on the ground to show where the crosswalks are.  These are at right angles (depending on which road you are crossing at the intersection) and, in between the two, there is a raised concrete block right on the corner.  That block has no marking on it at all, making it kind of invisible, particularly with sunglasses.  I didn’t see that there was a step.  Suddenly I was just  flying onto the ground in the bright sunshine on the hard concrete sidewalk and trying to protect my head to avoid hurting myself severely.

Although it was a dramatic fall, and somebody came running over right away from the miel-selling place, I was actually okay.  Maybe I bruised my elbow just a little bit.  But how funny that my first fall on the John Muir Trail should occur while walking without a pack in the bright sunshine of downtown Independence, California.

There are two places that advertise Mexican food in Independence, but the first one I visited was only open Monday to Friday and this was a Sunday.  The other was a taco truck pop-up next to the Shell station.  I had two carnitas, one asada, and one chorizo there, all really good tacos with a Jarritos de Mandarina (a Mexican tangerine-flavored soft drink) to wash them down.  It was wonderful.

Since I was still close to my motel, I ordered dinner and breakfast to go.  I got a dinner burrito of carnitas asadas, and a breakfast burrito of chorizo for the morning.  I put those in my hotel room and then headed out to the Eastern Sierra Ice Cream Company.

I swear the pure lime they sell there is absolutely the best.  I tried the orange one, which is supposed to be similar, but the lime was just better, so very tart.  This flavor was especially welcome because it was hot.

The temperature was “only” in the low to mid-90s, but the sun was just blasting down.  No one else was foolish enough to walk around town like I was.

Still, I enjoyed the chance to sight-see and I took some pictures of the town.  It was still the Inyo County seat, attesting to a former dynamism.  My picture of that distinguished building — the Inyo County Courthouse — tops this blog post.  But now the town was just dead.  It was weird.

It felt like a ghost town.  Here we were, in peak tourist season too, so it was very strange.  Though I did encounter an attractive young woman and almost persuaded her to come back to my room with me.  At least she let me take a photo of the two of us together which you can see below.

Back in my room (alone) I took stock.  No, I was not ALL better yet.  But I was much better than I had been and was finally trending toward recovery.  I had taken two ‘Zero’ days and would be falling out of alignment with my John Muir Trail permit if I took any more.  With some trepidation, I called Mark and arranged for a pickup at the motel the next morning at 6 a.m.

“Here I come,” I thought.  “I’m going back on the trail tomorrow.  At least, I’m going to try.  I have a 2,700-foot pass to climb right off the bat, so that will be a good test.  And if I can only make 2,500 feet of that, I can still turn around.  I can still come back down.”

I realized also that once I got over the pass, and headed into the High Sierra, I would be kind of committed to keeping on.  The “bail-out” points were few and challenging.  A couple of days earlier I did not expect to be on my way back to Kearsarge Pass, that was for sure.  But now I was going to try.

There was a lot to do before turning in.  I ate the dinner burrito.  It was enormous.  I guessed my hiker hunger was abating, because I couldn’t even finish it.

In assembling my gear, I could not find one of my canteens.  I looked everywhere.  Maybe it was in Sam’s rental car?  Sam gave me his Smartwater bottle, so I still had two water containers.  But I wanted to keep that canteen as it was easier to fill with a filtering squeeze bottle.

What else?  I took a shower, texted, sent emails, and called a bunch of people:  wife, son, friends.

I trimmed my nails a little bit.  They weren’t too long, but the shower presented an opportunity to trim them now.  Who knows whether or when I would be able to do it again the rest of the trip?

The hair tie holding my ponytail I did not even try to remove.  I accepted that my hair was already a complete rat’s nest and it was only going to get worse.

In my supply bucket was an alternate finger splint.  I wore a splint religiously on trail, trying to recover from a mallet finger sustained on my longest and hardest training hike.  In Independence I threw out the old splint and replaced it with the new one.

I packed my backpack.  That was challenging.  I love my backpack, but it was actually just a little too small for what I was carrying on this trip.  Adding the bear cannister crossed the tipping point.  Somehow, I was still making it work.

I tested my umbrella.  I thought, “If I can get that sun umbrella to work, it could actually help me a lot.”

With my new-and-untested 20,000 mAh power bank charged I had taken care of my electronics (except for the “untested” part).

I even spent a little time memorizing lines for my role in “Almost, Maine.”  Lee and I were slated to perform in that play after my return.

All this activity was exhausting me.  So, I completed these trail notes, set my alarm, and hit the mattress.  As I dozed off, I thought, “I hope my next set of trail notes convey a successful first day back on the trail…”

She and I had similar political views.  Indeed… “Make Pupusas, Not War”

#8322. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8319. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8317. New Hampshire

The penultimate state! Wow. Not only did it feel amazing to leave Vermont (finally!) but walking into such a highly anticipated state was surreal. Also Singe’s home state and homecoming! Even though I had never hiked in a lot of the prior states, I had at least visited a majority of them. But from the moment I stepped foot into New Hampshire, everything was brand new to me. I was trying to convey that New Hampshire and Maine would be new states for me but what I ended up saying was, “New state forever. Or…wait. How would a normal person say that?” To which Loon said, “How about ‘I’ve never been here before.'” lol.

Singe, Loon, and I walked across the Connecticut River into New Hampshire on a sweltering summer day in early August. Our first order of business? Jump right into the river. Before strolling into Hanover, right after the bridge, you can take a left, walk to the Dartmouth dock, ignore all the signs about it being for students and staff only, and jump right in. It felt AMAZING. I cannot emphasize enough how hot the sun was and how exposed the concrete bridge is. The river was full of weird cold pockets that we enjoyed to the max. Once we had cooled down, we finally walked into Hanover! I was super excited because I’m a little nerd who loves college campuses and Hanover being both a college town and a hiker town had always stuck with me.

Hanover was so cute and Dartmouth was so beautiful. Shocking. We found the Dartmouth Outdoors Club and left our packs in their care. Then we walked around Hanover and cashed in on some awesome hike friendly deals! We got free pizza for hikers and were completely entranced by the Housecleaning Games on ESPN 8: The Ocho. My favorite part? A poster that said “Ouchtown: Population YOU.” Incredible. We got handmade ice cream at Red Kite Candy which remains one of my most memorable ice cream stops on trail. I had Strawberry Balsamic. Thank you for asking. We grabbed our packs and walked around campus a little before getting picked up to stay with one of Singe’s good friends in town. It was so exciting to get a look into Singe’s life and meet the characters and friends she’s been talking about all trail!

We had an awesome night getting to know one of Singe’s oldest friends and having a homemade pot roast. YUM. Also this night, I got an email that I got off the waitlist for a marathon the first weekend of October. In Connecticut I started toying with the idea of running a marathon after trail just to see what would happen. When I received this email offering me a spot, I went for it. Turns out, this is the same marathon that Loon’s friend, who we have seen multiple times on trail, was training for! Done and done. The rest of the hike, this marathon was a sort of bit. I would forget I signed up and someone would mention it and I’d be like “oh RIGHT! The marathon! Yes, of course.” What a bit.

The next day, we were able to leave most of our things at Singe’s friend’s house because we were staying with another Singe friend connection the next night! We walked over Velvet Rocks, right off the campus of Dartmouth, and to our pick up spot near the Ice Cream Man’s house where I discovered my new favorite Key Lime popsicle. We got to hang out with the cutest dog’s at Singe’s friend’s parents’ house and enjoy their company and a delicious home-cooked meal.

We were back to it with full packs this time. We were coming up close to Singe’s house and sections of trail she’s done several times. The plan was for Loon and I to spend the night out on trail but Singe was going to get picked up by her partner and stay at her house. We would join them the next day. It feels weird to be apart from Singe for even a night but I loved having a night with just Loon. We plotted to stay at Hexacuba Shelter because it seems weird and cool. Like I’ve said many times before, you have to look for reasons to get excited for the day. Hexacuba is a shelter in a hexagon shape with a pentagon shaped privy. Obviously, we had to see that. It turned out to be just the two of us at the shelter that night so we threw up our tents inside to have some protection from the bugs. We had the sweetest night camping and laughing together.

We climbed up and over Smarts Mountain and onto the fire tower the day before Hexacuba and Cube Mountain the morning after Hexacuba. I loved both! On top of Cube Mountain, we found a rude comment someone had left on a post of mine that had been shared and honestly had a field day with it. This person’s mean comment (and others they would continue to leave on my posts later) became one of our tramily’s favorite inside jokes. We took it well and not seriously but a little reminder: If you don’t have anything nice to say, don’t say it! This can really hurt people! Especially online!

Anywho! After clearing these two mountains, covering more ground, and taking a perfect midday lake swim, Singe picked us up and we went back to her house! It was so fun to see where our trail bestie lived after talking about it for so many miles. Spoiler: It’s beautiful. We took a zero with her and got to see some of New Hampshire that’s off trail too. I didn’t know I was going to fall in love with New Hampshire so quickly! There was a lot of anticipation because as soon as we left the comfiness of Singe’s house, we would be entering the Whites. But of course we were able to scheme a slack-pack and were able to not bring full packs over Mt Moosilauke by dropping our things off at The Notch Hostel a day early.

I was quite nervous and intimidated of the Whites before we started. But step by step, we ascended the mountain. I actually flew up to the top pretty fast. It’s difficult, but I think I had it built up so much in my mind that it was better than I expected. I did fall in a little tiny creek on the way up (lol) but it didn’t get me down. And when I broke the treeline? I was so speechless and energized that nothing really mattered. I kept squealing to myself out of excitement. The terrain is gorgeous and we had a beautiful day. I loved being able to see the path ahead of me and the progress I was making pushing to the summit. There were a ton of people hiking at the top but I was in my own little world taking it all in…until I heard a group to my left singing out “You’re a bear and I’m a girlllll.” AKA the Song of the Summer AKA the song I sang to a bear when I had a close encounter back in New York. I looked over and our trail cousins, The Binguses were sitting together serenading me. What a welcome to the top! This was the first of several mountain top reunions that kept happening in the Whites. So much fun. I went over and had lunch with them and waited for Singe and Loon to summit. We hadn’t seen the Binguses since we were all in New York City together in early July! We also got to meet a new Bingus they’d picked up along the way in Vermont.

We all hung out together at the top. Apparently some kind of eclipse was happening but not a full eclipse so we didn’t end up sticking around to see it from the top since the weather looked like it might be turning too. We all bunched up together for a picture on the summit that a day hiker took. It looked like she was taking several. She said to us, “How many do you want?” So we figured we’d have good options. But when she returned the phone, we had exactly three pictures. lol. Us Golden Girls and the Binguses all tackled the steep and endless descent together. We stopped a few times to look at the pretty waterfalls that follow the trail. It was so fun to be back with them again for this hike. We all got to the parking lot and waited for the shuttle to the Notch. A few of the Binguses weren’t staying at the hostel so they found a hitch into town.

We got picked up to head to the Notch by the owner, Serena, who also happens to be Singe’s good friend and climbing partner in normal life! She was awesome! Please stay at the Notch! They are so great and have their systems figured out so smoothly. Serena told the 6 of us in the shuttle (3 Golden Girls + 3 of the Binguses) that a local outdoor apparel company, Burgeon, wanted to invite 6 hikers for a pan pasta dinner tonight. So of course we were like, “we’ll we’re 6 hikers…” And voila! We checked in, showered, and an hour later we were on our way to have one of the best meals of my life. Three workers at Burgeon ate with us in their on-site stock room. They were cool and fun and we had a great time. This was one of the coolest and most exciting trail magics we had. Loon asked if they needed a Colorist to work for them since I work in fashion as a colorist! Thanks for trying to get me a job, Loon!

After the dinner, Singe’s partner offered to pick us up and take us to Super Secret Ice Cream. An ice cream shop in Bethlehem, NH that Singe had been talking up since probably day 2 of me knowing her. As an ice cream connoisseur and an AT Dairy-Blazer, I couldn’t wait. We left the boy Binguses behind and Loon, Singe, Outlaw, and I got ice cream. I am absolutely obsessed with this place. The branding, the colors, the unique small-batch flavors, the ice cream flights, the posters–all of it is perfect. New favorite ice cream. I think it’s extremely tragic that I live so far away from it and also probably for the best. If you’re even remotely close though, take the detour! Best ice cream I’ve had on trail and also in years hands down.

All of this together made for such a magical day and one of the standouts from trail. Tackling a hard and anticipated mountain but feeling strong? That view?! Reuniting with our friends unexpectedly! Surprise trail magic pasta dinner?! AND SUPER SECRET ICE CREAM?! What a way to kick off the Whites.

The next day we slackpacked the Kinsmens with The Notch. They have a deal that if you stay two nights, the slackpack is included. Yes please! The Kinsmens were some of the most difficult parts of the Whites. It wasn’t my worst day there, but quite a challenge. The final ascent up is basically bouldering/rock scrambling. I was so glad to not have my full pack weight, but I did feel extremely rushed trying to catch the shuttle back to the Notch. The options were a 4pm or 7pm. We got a tiny bit of a later start that ate into our hiking time. Thus, I ended my hike around 4:10pm while feeling extremely rushed and stressed the last part of the day. The trail was super rocky and frustrating. We missed the shuttle but since Singe did know the staff well, they came and picked us up. Thank you! When we got back to the hostel, someone had decided to make dinner for everyone as trail magic. What a godsend. Two covered dinners in a row. I was so incredibly exhausted after the Kinsmens that I probably would have cried if I had to figure out my own dinner. Moosilauke felt like a warm up but the Kinsmens felt like an ass-kicking. I was worried more of that was to come but Singe told me she thinks the Kinsmens are some of the hardest 4kers in the Whites and it shouldn’t feel worse than that which really helped. Tomorrow, we’d be back to full packs and really getting into it!

There is a challenge in New Hampshire hiking called the New Hampshire 48. This refers to a group of 48 prominent peaks all above 4k. The AT goes right over a few of them, and grazes along the side of a few others. Some people choose to tag the summits and take the detours to hit as many summits as they can. In hiking this pursuit of summits is called “Peak Bagging.” While we went through the Whites, Loon was all in on peak bagging as many of the 48 as she could. She was a rockstar! Singe and I supported her and encouraged her but did not have the same drive. I was too worried about my ankles on all the rocky ups and downs that I didn’t want to risk anything by doing extras. Because of this, Singe and I sometimes had slightly different days than Loon. Like for example, when Loon walked an extra like 7 miles to get 4 extra peaks in a day and Singe and I walked 5 extra miles the next day to be able to go get ice cream. It’s important to know where your priorities are.

Still, on the AT, I got my fair share of the 48 done. The trail follows a section of the Whites called the Pemigewasset Loop (or Pemi Loop) for about 10 miles after the Kinsmens. Most notably, it follows along Franconia Ridge which is an exposed ridge walk that goes over multiple peaks. You can see the circle of the Pemi Loop through the mountains while up on the ridge. I absolutely loved Franconia Ridge. It’s like nothing else on the trail. It most closely reminded my of a hike I had done in the Dolomites! And yet it’s here! Just sitting up in New Hampshire! Wow! Franconia is known for being beautiful but also extreme due to the exposure. Like everything in the Whites, it’s quite steep (like straight up rock ladders for miles) to get up to the top and then open to strong winds and weather with nowhere to hide. We were lucky to have gorgeous weather throughout the Whites. While we did have some wind (including being pushed over by the wind a few times), it was nothing unmanageable or unpleasant on Franconia. Still, the exposure is tough. There was even a Search and Rescue on this section the same day we were up there. But we got through it just fine along with my new can of Honey Mustard Pringles that we became obsessed with and didn’t last more than 6 miles. We were in such awe the whole time. When I first got to the top of the ridge, I ran into McMurphy! Another mountain top reunion! Loon started a little further back to get more peaks, so we also reunited with her on a summit!

Towards the end of the ridge, the novelty had worn off a little and we were ready to get out of the wind and set up camp for the night. We went down and then up and over Mount Garfield where I had another summit reunion! I ran into Sniper, a woman I had met in Georgia and North Carolina. She hiked the AT years ago and is attempting a Yo-yo of the full trail this year! This means she hiked from Georgia to Maine and will turn around and hike all the way back down to Georgia. Incredible!! It was so cool to run into her and see her still crushing it! After leaving her and wishing her the best on the rest of the journey, I made my way down to the Garfield Campsite where of course we ran into several other friends!

The Whites are known for their Hut-to-Hut system where you can stay in little lodges along the way. This is awesome for a stand alone trip, but not really an option for thru-hikers. They are quite expensive (especially multiple nights in a row) and require reservations far in advance. That would be nearly impossibly to schedule on a thru-hiker’s flexible and ever-changing timeline. Stealth camping is also not allowed/highly discouraged in the Whites due to the extreme weather and the delicate nature of the alpine plants. There are designated campgrounds throughout the Whites that each have caretakers. They are all first come first serve, but the caretakers are great at finding spots for everyone so we were never too stressed about it. At this first campsite, we registered for a thru-hiker pass with the caretaker that allows us to camp at all the campgrounds for a discounted price and also get free pastries and soup when we stop into the huts! Wahoo! We opted to stay in the shelter the first night because of the wind.

The next day we started off our hike by basically having to walk straight down a sort of rocky waterfall. The Whites are on another level. We made it to the Galehead Hut for lunch where we cashed in our free soup pass. Then we continued up South Twin Mountain. For some reason, when we summited, I could not get “Breathe” by Faith Hill out of my head and I continued to sing it as my anthem the rest of trail. South Twin was a long push up, but the descent felt flat compared to the climb. What a treat! We went to a campsite a little off the path since there weren’t too many options otherwise. You’d either have to do a really short day or a really long one. Given the strenuous terrain, we opted for a short day. Singe and I got to the campsite around 3pm while Loon went off to go bag three more peaks! It felt really nice to have time to relax and recover. I don’t think I got to camp before 4pm since North Carolina. We stayed in the shelter this night too and watched a beautiful sunrise from the comfort of our sleeping bags the next morning.

Our next day in the Whites was a bit of a Choose Your Own Adventure. This was one of the only nights on trail (the only night on trail?) that Singe, Loon, and I were all apart. I had a field day telling people we were all apart because we were fighting. Nobody believed it for a second. We had a bit of an easier day planned passing by Zealand Hut and aiming for Ethan Pond Shelter. But Singe’s friend told us she could meet us at the trailhead for Zealand Hut and take us to lunch in Bethlehem and then return us to trail. Loon decided to pass and stick with the original plan since she was already doing so many extra miles and peaks but all Singe had to tell me was we could get Super Secret Ice Cream again and I was in. Singe left a little before me in the morning but we met up at Zealand Hut. It was super special to be there with her because it was the first place she decided she ever wanted to Thru-Hike back in college. <3 We took a side trail that was super flat about 2.5 miles to a parking lot. I timed myself on how long it took from Zealand to the lot because I had the idea that I might try to return later for Work-For-Stay if the timing worked out. We had a great lunch and ice cream of course and were returned to the trailhead. It felt like we snuck off campus in the middle of the day with our cool older sister. We were cutting it close but I wanted to try for the work for stay at Zealand since it’s a unique thru-hiker experience and I didn’t know when else the timing would work out to try. I ZOOMED through the 2.5 miles back up to Zealand in record time and ta-da! I was granted one of the three work for stay spots that night! Singe ended up camping solo sort of in between Loon at Ethan Pond and myself at the hut.

Two more hikers I knew rolled in and we hung around the pretty waterfall waiting for our duties to begin. We got leftovers from the dinner that night and then were assigned the tasks of sweeping, wiping down tables, and reorganizing the freezer for the hut croo. In exchange, we got the dinner leftovers and were able to sleep in the dining room which was much appreciated since it rained that night. We had to get up super early so the staff could make breakfast for the paying guests. We hung around outside until breakfast leftovers were set out and then we descended on those. From there we made our way to the AMC Highland Center where Loon, Singe, and I met back up for a zero. I had a job interview over the phone the next day and I was touched by Singe and Loon’s efforts to make sure we were somewhere I could take the call with reliable service. We were excited for a rest too since the Whites are so demanding even when dropping the number of miles you’re doing each day. The Highland Center was also super neat because we got to run into our friend, Mosey, who we met during the first half of trail and was an original Bingus! The Binguses also trickled in over the next day and we got to catch up with them as well!

The interview went well (though did not ultimately land me a job…but that’s story for Maine) and I was feeling excited. There was no laundry so we did our best to freshen our clothes up in the bunkhouse sink. We enjoyed taking over the on-site library to do our nails and watch TV on our phones together. It was nice to have a little break before the Presidential Range or “The Prezies.” We actually lucked out by taking a zero for my interview because it let some bad weather pass and gave us a perfect weather window later!

After our time at the Highland Center and mapping out our next stretch, we made our way back up into the range. We made our way to the Mizpah Hut and Nauman Campground. Mizpah was one of my favorite huts. There was something more remote, cozy, and mellow about it more than the others I had seen. The Croo was also very friendly. We checked on a work-for-stay just to see but they didn’t have any so we camped at the Nauman Campground next door. Singe, Loon, and I got an entire tenting platform to ourselves! We didn’t know it then, but this would be the last night the three of us would camp together without anyone else. We had a magical time. Somehow, it wasn’t too cold so we decided to cowboy camp on our platform under the clear sky. We watched a beautiful sunset and had such a fun and special night. We were laughing so much. This night was such a highlight on trail. We slept under the stars and I remember waking up at different times during the night and seeing how the milky way was moving across the sky. What an experience.

The next day we got breakfast leftovers at Mizpah Hut with another female hiker who was traveling with her partner. I think she enjoyed having some girl time with us and we loved it too! We made our way from the hut up to the Mount Pierce summit (President Pierce not Pierce Brosnan apparently) and were officially in the Prezies! The first summit was not so bad but we were hyped! We could see the others stretching before us, most of which we’d tackle that day! We took a moment at the summit to talk about how excited we were. Before we continued on, Singe said, “Does anyone have words they’d like to share about Pierce before we continue?” which made me laugh all day thinking about it.

Mount Eisenhower was next and it was so beautiful! We had a gorgeous day and could see Mount Washington’s summit for the first time! Though it was quite windy, Eisenhower was one of my favorite mountains in the Prezies because the 360 views are so stunning! What a view of Washington! After a snack break and some photos, we kept it moving before getting too cold. We went up and over Little Monroe and Mount Monroe where we got a look at Lakes of the Clouds Hut where we would be staying. We decided to go ahead and book a full guest spot for Lakes of the Clouds because we wanted to experience the hut culture as guests and because it’s tricky to find a place to camp if you show up to this hut and there’s no room for thru hikers. Everything is exposed and there’s no camping around. By this point, you’re at the base of Mount Washington and frankly, out of options. We felt like we had such a magical day hopping from summit to summit and squealing about the views and the weather. Also, mileage wise, Lakes of the Clouds is not so far from Nauman Campground so we made it to the hut in really good time. Such good time, in fact, that we decided to go ahead and summit Mount Washington that afternoon! Originally we were going to wait until the next day but when you get good weather and you have the time…don’t waste that opportunity. We decided to go up the 1.5 trail to the summit with slackpacks and take a trail around the next day.

Washington was….fine. Loon, Singe, and I pressed play on the Hamilton soundtrack at the same time to get us up the mountain. It’s so strange to make your way up this infamous beast of a mountain only to be met with a bunch of ill prepared tourists who drove or took the Cog Railroad up. It was crowded and touristy, but hey, at least we weren’t hit with 100mph winds! We didn’t stay terribly long before making our way back to the hut. We knew 3 of the Binguses were making their way to the hut tonight too and we were excited to see them. Our friend, Mosey, was also able to work on-site at Lakes of the Clouds that day and spend the night too! The Binguses had to come from further so they had more of an exhausting day but and were wiped. Still, it was great to see them and spend some time with them after dinner when everyone went outside to take in one of our best sunsets of trails. I heard Brewski say, “We got to do stars tonight” about remembering to stargaze and it cracked me up enough that that phrase became a part of our lexicon the rest of trail.

While the first half of the Prezies were a dream, the second half were a bit of a nightmare. I did not enjoy day two of the traverse. The landscape was completely exposed all day and so rocky and unstable. It felt endless and frustrating. Maybe everything we’d been doing physically caught up to me and the novelty wore off? Either way, yikes. We made our way around Washington towards Jefferson where I did decide to tag the summit even though it was technically off trail. I got to the top and felt very regretful that I wasted the effort. I did not go up to tag Mount Adams. We made our way to Madison Hut where we ran into half of the Binguses again and commiserated about the day with them. I remember us telling Brewski “Can you please fake a medical emergency so we can all get airlifted out? You’re still on your parents’ insurance so it has to be you.”

We were trying to explore other options or side trails for getting down. We were going to meet Singe’s parents this night and stay with them in an airbnb and zero the next day but the idea of having a bed to sleep in felt too far away while we were traversing around. We wanted very badly to not have to go up and over Mount Madison and down to Pinkham Notch but there was really no other route. Eventually, we just had to go. The ascent up Madison really wasn’t so awful but the trail down? If you can even call it a trail? Was the absolute worst part of the entire AT for me. Everything was so exposed and unstable and endless and I felt like I would be stuck on the mountain forever. The progress was glacial and the steps were slow. I was without a doubt angry hiking. I remember looking for any sliver of hope and saying, “It’s only .9 left to the treeline!” and Loon, the beautiful and literal hiker she is, said, “And then it gets even steeper!” To which I yelled something like, “SHUT UP WHY WOULD YOU SAY THAT TO ME?!” We weren’t really angry at each other and it’s a moment we laughed about a lot throughout the rest of trail. I seriously think the descent down Madison is extremely dangerous and I cannot believe it isn’t talked about more. ANYWAYS. We did get down to the treeline and for me and my knees, it felt at least a little better walking on dirt and having trees to cling to if it was too steep.

We made it down to the Osgood Campsite where a random man appeared out of nowhere and tried to give me unsolicited advice. I was not having it. We kept joking that throughout this hike our faith in humanity has gone up but our tolerance of men has gone down. Once Singe and Loon made it down too, we took the original AT instead of the detour so that we could make it to Pinkham Notch for Singe’s parents to pick us up. What looked flat on the map ended up being flat with some random sharp ups and downs. Normally this would be okay, but when we’re already feeling so worn out, this was maddening. One of Singe’s friends had originally planned to meet us SOBO during the hike but wasn’t able to make it all the way up so she left us a bag of trail magic which we found towards the end of the day. It was a really sweet mental boost. We were about .2 from the Mount Washington Auto Road and 2 miles from Pinkham Notch. It was almost 7pm and we knew we were losing daylight quickly. Loon ran ahead to see if we could hitch down to the auto road entrance with the last of the cars leaving Mount Washington. The road up closes at 6pm but we hoped we could catch a hitch from some stragglers on the way out. We saw exactly two cars. One was a minivan that slowed down to tell us they didn’t have room even though we could clearly see they did. I started to cry. The next was a truck. I continued to pathetically cry while we asked for a ride to hopefully sway the decision. Unfortunately, it was a Washington worker who wasn’t allowed to give a ride in the work vehicle. We completely understood and that was disappointing but fine with us. The real kick in the pants was actually when he said, “The quickest thing for you to do will be to take the AT 2 miles down to Pinkham Notch.” WE KNOW SIR! My knees and feet were beat to crap from the day and I knew I didn’t have two more trail miles in the dark in me. We decided to walk down the auto road to where Singe’s dad could pick us up.

Loon, Singe, and I stayed in an airbnb with Singe’s parents near North Conway. We had a zero where we got our errands done and were also able to do a big fat nothing. Thank you Mr. & Mrs. Singe for your generosity once again!! The Binguses also took a zero at Mosey’s so we were all aligned for the next stretch! On Sunday, we set back out for the stretch between The Wildcats (where we listened to High School Musical) and the Carters (where I listened to Beyonce). We stayed overnight at Imp Shelter. The weather was drizzly but still could have been worse and was better than we expected. This is quite a steep section to do in the wet. Singe and I got to the shelter first so we watched Hacks on her phone before others showed up. I did spill an entire new bag of mini M&Ms but luckily my spirits were restored enough to think this was funny and not too tragic.

The next day, us Golden Girls and half of the Binguses hiked from Imp Shelter over Mount Moriah and down to the 1900 mile marker! We are right on the heels of Maine! We were greeted by The Ice Cream Man who gave us Klondike bars from his camper. We met some cool SOBOs and took pictures at the final 1900s mile marker before getting picked up by a friend I had made hiking out in the Dolomites last year. We met on a practice hike I did in Italy (I used practicing for the AT as an excuse to hike in really cool places and I recommend you do the same). I actually twisted my ankle (shocking) and he helped wrap it up since he is a SAR volunteer in the Whites! We got to talking while staying at some of the same huts and he told me to reach out when I came through on the AT and he and his wife would host me and whomever! It felt surreal to know this other milestone had been met. I was getting to see the New Hampshire connection I had before hiking.

My friend and his wife were so lovely and generous to us. We showered and enjoyed their company. My friend told us stories of his best SARs. We made taco bowls for them in exchange for the homestay and Strider made an apple pie from scratch!! The next day, we stayed talking over breakfast way longer than we planned because they were just so fun. My friend ended up letting me drive his car back to trail and leave a pin for him to pick it up later. Like I said, they were extremely generous to us. It felt a little funny to drive my trail friends in his car. We made it to the trail head and continued on! We had a long day pushing to the first shelter in Maine! We went up and over Mt Success which is the last mountain in New Hampshire. At the top, we learned the news that Dolly Parton had died. RIP. We also found one of our favorite FarOut comments on trail. If you scroll to the very beginning of the Mt Success comments it says “take that Dad!” Nice.

Soon we crossed into Maine! It immediately became about 10x more extreme just like everyone had promised. But also 10x more breathtaking. We saw a double rainbow while crossing over the Goose Eye mountains which I like to think was for Dolly. I thought maybe I’d feel more emotional crossing into Maine. Certainly it’s a big moment, but there’s still a lot of work to be done. Still, I did it. At the very least, my legs and feet have taken me from Georgia to Maine.

#8316. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8312. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8310. Te Araroa day 10: My first zero day

0km, Amelia and Nathan’s house in Kerikeri

It was delightful to wake up in a bed – a double bed no less. I think the last time I slept in a double bed was in Vietnam in March! The sleep-out isn’t fully finished so there weren’t any curtains in my room, which was fine by me. I woke up before the sunrise anyway. The others had said they wanted a slow morning, so I spent quite a while in bed writing and uploading blog posts before anyone else was up. I also called my parents, who I hadn’t spoken to since before I started hiking. We had bought stuff for a shared breakfast the night before but eventually I was too hungry and couldn’t wait anymore, and ended up grabbing some toast.

When the others were up, we made breakfast and had a guided tour around Amelia and Nathan’s large garden. Seeing Nicole’s reaction to the house and garden remided me that I felt the same when I first arrived in NZ. I was really taken aback by the amount of land a lot of people have over here. In our small, densely populated bits of Europe (Nicole is Swiss) land is very expensive, and you would assume anyone with a garden that size was rather wealthy. But over here, I guess land is relatively cheap (outside of the main population centres anyway). So having big gardens or a paddock or two is much more common.

Then we all spent some time trying to plan the next section. Ruby was trying desperately to organise kayaking from Paihia to Waikare, but the person who would drive the kayaks back was away until Thursday. Nicole and I were trying to figure out how many days of food we would need, and where to stay. It was a challenge because the accommodation options aren’t all shown on the map, some are only in the ‘accomodation’ section of the trail notes, and some are even buried in the trail description. We were getting a bit frustrated at the lack of clarity from the TA app. Based on the mileage though, it was clear it would be quite a long stretch to the next ‘proper’ supermarket, a Four Square in Ruakaka. Four Squares are small local supermarkets usually found in smaller towns in NZ. They can be highly variable in terms of how big they are and what they sell, but TA hikers have to rely on them for resupply in quite a few places. After Paihia, we wouldn’t be hitting another big supermarket until Mangawhai, in over 200km.

Eventually we admitted defeat and decided to take about 5 days of food and plan the rest on the fly. There are enough small shops and dairies in between that we figured we would make it work. It was getting on for lunchtime and we needed to go to the gear shop and the supermarket.Ruby drove us into town and we went into Hunting and Fishing. I got a new headlamp, and I think Ruby needed gas. Then we headed across the road to Woolworths. I managed to get most of the things I wanted, although I find the Woolworths bulk section very lacking compared to New World and Pak’N Save. I got some food for lunch too, and Nicole and I bought some alcohol for Amelia and Nathan as a thank you.

We picked Zoe up in town, where she had been staying with some friends of friends, and headed down towards the Stone Store where we had finished our hike the previous day. Nicole had seen a slice she wanted but hadn’t been able to get it as the cafe was closing. We had a nice lunch by the river, then dropped Zoe off and headed ‘home’ to organise our resupplies.I was quite pleased with the amount of food I had. Actually, I started wondering if I should have got more!

Later in the afternoon, the others all went for a swim but I wanted to continue doing my blog posts. I’d been so far behind and it was feeling good to catch up. I got a couple of posts done by the time the others came back, and when they were done showering we headed over to the main house to make pizzas. It was a nice evening and cool to get to know Amelia and Nathan a bit – and hear some of their stories from outdoor adventures with Ruby and Matt! After dinner I spoke to a friend on the phone, and eventually went to bed.

#8308. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub
