#8285. Best Lever Action Rifles of 2026

Published Oct 27, 2026 12:56 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When I was a kid, there were three reasons I wanted a lever action rifle. First, they were cool. Second, because I grew up just outside New Haven, Conn., the historic home to Marlin and Winchester, they were my hometown guns. Third, they were cheap.

Only one of these things is still true. Lever guns always have been and always will be cool, though they will never again be cheap, nor—barring divine intervention—will they ever again be produced in Gun Valley.

Writing about the top lever action rifles is a bit tricky. Do you focus on the best of all time, which is great for us nostalgic sorts, or do you talk about great lever action rifles that you can buy new?

I tilted this list of the best lever action rifles in favor of those you can order new. Though if you have a hankering for one of the old-time classics, there are plenty to be had on the used market. Just don’t expect to find any bargains. Nearly all quality lever actions command a premium.

This list is divided into those guns that are being currently produced (or soon-to-be) in significant numbers and those that are either specialty orders or that must be sought out on the used gun market.

With the exception of the rifles that have just been announced, Senior Staff Writer Tyler Freel and I have shot, handled, and/or owned all the models listed. Beyond our hands-on experience with the rifles over the years, however, many of them are no-brainers based on their well-documented history and legacy.

The good — actually, great — news here is that we’re seeing more lever actions made with each passing year. About 15 years ago, Remington screwed the pooch with Marlin and those were some dark days indeed. In those years it seemed only Henry was making quality lever guns in meaningful numbers, but things have taken a turn for the better.

Under Ruger’s ownership, Marlin seems poised to flourish. Henry is still innovating hard and trotting out new models in new cartridges, like the 360 Buckhammer. And we have a couple interesting and innovative newcomers in the mix.

When Ruger resurrected Marlin, the first model they brought back was the 1895 SBL. This was a smart move because the SBL, with its gray laminate furniture, stainless steel metal, threaded barrel, oversized lever loop, and picatinny rail was one of the sexiest and most sought-after iterations of this classic lever action.

I had good things to say about the Marlin 1895 SBL when it was reintroduced in late 2021, and that opinion hasn’t shifted. It is the best lever action rifle produced under the Marlin brand—at least in the modern era. Packing 6+1 rounds of .45/70 Gov’t in its magazine, it brings a formidable level of firepower to the party which is why it has garnered a lot of interest from hunters in bear country, as well as with everyday sportsmen in more sedate parts of the U.S.

Marlin has also introduced two new versions of the 1895 worth considering, a Model 1895 Trapper and a Model 1895 Guide Gun. The Trapper comes with a Skinner peep sight, no picatinny rail, and is a bit more compact (34 ¼ in. vs. 37 ¼ in.) than the SBL. It, too, is chambered in .45/70 and has a 5+1 magazine capacity. The Guide Gun (model GBL) is slightly less expensive than the SBL ($1,239 vs. $1,479), has traditional semi-buckhorn sights, blued steel, is chambered in .45/70, and a 6+1 capacity.

In 2024, Smith & Wesson made a big splash in the lever-gun world with their model 1854. It was first introduced in .44 Magnum, and .45/70 models followed suit in 2025, along with options in the venerable .30/30 Winchester and .45 Colt.

We were immediately impressed by the first Model 1854 rifles we got our hands on. These lever guns, which are relatively complex pieces of machinery, were superbly executed — with excellent fit and finish and smooth operation. They feature both side-gate and magazine tube loading, and are available in blued/wood and stainless/synthetic trims. Both are generally classic-looking styles, but the synthetic version offers modern perks like a picatinny rail, M-Lok slots on the fore-end, and a threaded muzzle. Since introduction, Smith & Wesson have also introduced a Stealth Hunter model with black-on-black finish, a longer optic rail, tactical-style handguard with multiple M-Lok slots, and threaded muzzle — specifically for optics, lights, and a suppressor.

We’ve tested several of the Model 1854 rifles as they’ve rolled out and have been consistently impressed with the quality of build, smoothness of operation, and reliability of these guns. We rank them among the finest factory lever guns made today.

One of the slickest, funnest lever guns we’ve ever run is the Lever Action Supreme from Henry. This rifle combines the nostalgia and classic good looks of a lever gun with some features that a lot of modern shooters will find appealing. It’s offered in both 5.56/.223 and .300 Blackout, and its most notable characteristic is that it feeds from standard AR-15 magazines. Since it’s introduction, it’s also been updated to include the popular .450 Bushmaster. This isn’t simply a design that Henry adapted to work with these mags and cartridges. They started from scratch.

The Lever Action Supreme cycles very smoothly and uses an AR-style rotating bolt head and the bolt body does not protrude from the rear of the receiver as with many other lever guns when cycled. It also sports a floated barrel that provides good accuracy and while it has a classic look when bare, it’s equipped to accommodate modern accessories like suppressors, scopes, and red dot optics. You can read Snow’s full review of the Lever Action Supreme for a more detailed look.

It didn’t seem that long ago that Henry Repeating Arms was only making Golden Boys chambered in pistol cartridges and .22s. But these guys have been busy, and as the company embarks on its second quarter century, they have added an impressive number of products to the lineup.

One of the flagship hunting rifles is the All-Weather Picatinny Rail .45/70 Side Gate, which is Henry’s version of a do-everything guide gun. As the name implies, it is built for the elements. The metal has a hard-chrome satin finish. The stock is a stained hardwood.

It has an aperture peep sight mounted at the rear of the substantial Picatinny rail. Henry outfitted it with an oversized lever loop. With the 18.43-inch barrel, the overall length is 37.5 inches and it has a 4+1 capacity. The rifle can be loaded either through the side gate on the receiver or by dropping rounds into the tubular magazine.

This is a versatile and capable thumper that is equally at home in bear country or in a deer stand overlooking a food plot.

The Winchester Model 1873 might have been The Gun that Won the West—a great bit of marketing by Winchester executives—but the Model 94 is undeniably the rifle that won the hearts and minds of generations of deer hunters. If you polled long-time hunters regarding their choice as the top lever action rifle, there’s little doubt the Winchester 94 would win the vote.

This was the most prolific of Winchester’s lever actions, being the first sporting rifle in the U.S. to sell a million units. Prior to the end of its domestic production in 2006, more than seven million Model 94s were produced.

Model 94s are still being made for Browning/Winchester by Miroku Corp. in Japan and are available in several different grades. These run from the basic Carbine (1,309)withitsplainwalnutstockandbrushedpolishedbluedmetal,totheDeluxeSporting(2,230), which has case color hardened metalwork, upgraded wood, nicely executed checkering, and a half-round, half-octagonal deeply blued barrel.

Currently, the 94 is being offered in .30/30 Win., .38/55 and .450 Marlin.

The Browning BLR is one of the most versatile lever actions on the market. It is available in both short- and long-action lengths and because it feeds from a detachable box magazine it is able to run pointy spitzer-style bullets in cartridges usually associated with bolt guns.

The Lightweight ’81 Stainless Takedown is the most utilitarian BLR of them all, making it the best lever action rifle in the BLR family. It breaks down into two pieces for easy transport and is built on a lightweight aluminum receiver and sports a stainless steel barrel for excellent weather resistance. At about 7.25 pounds (depending on the specific chambering) it has a very nice balance and feel. Combined with its smooth lever system, which uses a clever gear and pinion design, the BLR embodies the lithe, fast-handling characteristics that lever action fans admire. (I’d be remiss if I didn’t give a nod to the legendary Winchester Model 88, which was a game-changing lever action from which the BLR drew lots of inspiration.)

The Lightweight ’81 Takedown is currently chambered in .243 Win., 6.5 Creedmoor, 7mm-08 Rem., .308 Win., .300 WSM, .30/06, and .300 Win. Mag. Several other cartridges are available in other BLR models as well.

It’s difficult for me to express how happy I am to include the Marlin 336 among the top lever action rifles currently made. I know I’m not alone in this. I cut my teeth hunting deer with a Marlin 336 in .35 Remington so, as with countless other hunters, the 336 was my first love.

We’ve handled and put a few rounds through one of the new 336’s, which will initially be chambered in .30/30 Win., and its quality was spot-on. As with the 1895s, the 336s have excellent fit and finish, run smoothly, and are aesthetically pleasing.

As you history buffs probably know, the original Henry lever action was the first commercially successful lever action rifle. Originally chambered in .44 Rimfire, it was one of the most advanced firearms to see action during the Civil War and was fielded in limited numbers by Union Troops.

Confederate Colonel John Mosby is credited with cursing it as “that damned Yankee rifle that can be loaded on Sunday and fired all week,” after fighting against troops wielding it in battle. That unintentional endorsement stuck and helped propel the Henry to everlasting fame.

Henry makes a “New Original Henry” chambered in either .44-40 WCF or .45 Colt, though the most popular (and affordable) homage is the Henry Golden Boy rimfire, which can be had in .22 S/L/LR, .22 Mag., or .17 HMR.

In .22 LR, the most popular configuration, the rifle holds 16 rounds, the same as the original. It has a 20-inch octagonal barrel that is nicely blued and contrasts sharply with the bright “Brasslite” finished receiver and brass buttpad and barrel band.

The receiver comes drilled and tapped for a scope, but before you mount an optic on yours spend some time running it with semi-buckhorn sights, as the Creator intended.

These Golden Boys run like a scalded squirrel and can digest ammo by the brick over the course of an afternoon.

As a first gun for a youngster, it has no real equal. But its appeal is so strong that no one will fault you for buying one for your grownup self first.

In 2024, Savage introduced the Revel, a rimfire lever-action chambered in .22 LR, .22 WMR, and .17 HMR. Considering their modest price, these are great little lever actions. They come in three trims: Classic, DLX, and Tactical.

I’ve had one of the classic Revels for a couple years and it’s a wonderful balance of traditional looks, performance, and modern features. It’s got handsome walnut furniture with a couple of modern lines and nice ergonomics. The steel has a matte blued finish, and the aluminum receiver is coated in black as well. The DLX has wood furniture with some modern M-Lok slots and the gun has a threaded muzzle. The Tactical version has black synthetic furniture.

The classic version I’ve been shooting has traditional dovetailed sights and the slightly heavy weight of the barrel, in conjunction with the buttstock design, makes the rifle quick to the shoulder and steady pointing. The receiver is unique in that it features two push pins that can be used to take the rifle down in seconds for stowage or cleaning. A lot of our .22 LR ammo is excessively waxy, and that can gum up lever guns pretty easily so easy takedown is helpful.

The Tactical Revel comes with a Picatinny rail for mounting an optic, but the other models are drilled and tapped to accommodate a scope. These are some of the nicer rimfire lever guns you’ll find for the money today.

The Marlin 1894 was hot stuff when it was introduced back in the day. It was the first lever gun with a flat top, side-eject design that anticipated the eventual wide-spread adoption of telescopic sights on rifles. This innovation gave it a leg up (on paper anyway) compared to the Winchester 1894 which debuted at the same time, though the fact that the Winchester came in the potent .30/30 versus the less powerful offerings in the Marlin gave Winchester’s 1894 a decisive advantage.

The Marlin 1894 has been chambered in a variety of mostly pistol-caliber cartridges over the decades, the most common of which (in the modern era) included the .44 Spl./.44 Magnum. .38 Spl./.357 Magnum and .45 Colt. I have a North Haven, Conn., built 1894 in .44 Magnum and it is one of my favorite carbines. (Though if I could snap my fingers and conjure any 1894 it would be one chambered in the quaint and now obsolete .218 Bee.)

Ruger announced the return of the Marlin 1894 this spring, so we will hopefully have hands-on range time with one soon for a full review. Expect to see the first offerings in the cartridges mentioned above, but as details become available we’ll update this information. (Note: the rifle pictured above is one of the older Marlin 1894s).

Rossi has recently, with the R95, become a true contender in the .45/70 lever gun space. Their stainless-steel R95 Laminate .45/70 is a high-quality gun that incorporates some modernized features and is better quality than even some of the previous Marlin models. This model has a polished stainless receiver — that is honestly a bit over-polished — and laminated wood furniture. They seem durable and weather-resistant in our testing, but we’d prefer the fit of the fore end to be a bit better. The sides of it aren’t fully against the magazine tube and can flex and potentially crack.

This new .45/70 lever gun features a modernized M16-style extractor and a threaded muzzle for accepting a suppressor. Staff writer Tyler Freel put a lot of ammo through his sample and it ran beautifully. You can read his full review here. Priced below some of the top-shelf lever guns like the new Marlin, Henry, and Smith & Wesson rifles, it’s affordable but still very good quality.

Another great Rossi lever gun is the Rio Bravo .22 LR. This is available in a number of configurations, but we really like the wood/gold variant. This is a lever gun with good looks that isn’t priced to be a safe queen. Staff Writer Tyler Freel put one of these to the test with his son and you can read his full review here.

The Rio Bravo has an aluminum receiver with a top cover that’s held in place with four Phillips-head screws. It’s easily removed for cleaning and maintenance — something that’s important to keep rimfire lever guns working correctly. It’s an accurate rifle that works well with a variety of ammunition and holds 14 rounds in its tubular magazine. If you want to mount an optic, you can use the narrow dovetail atop the receiver with tip-off rings, but this gun is most fun with iron sights.

This list could have been much longer, but in the interest of brevity I’ve only highlighted a few notable classic lever guns. Before getting to those, however, I do want to highlight a couple important honorable mentions.

The Spencer repeating rifle is one. It was the first military repeating rifle that used self-contained metallic cartridges and is the forefather of all lever actions. Though the Spencer was produced for only a short time (1860 to 1869) and in relatively limited numbers, it was the steppingstone upon which the lever action rifle, specifically Winchesters, was built.

The Winchester 1895, which gained prominence as Teddy Roosevelt’s “Big Medicine” in .405 Winchester is an iconic lever action whose fame outstrips its actual benefits. From a technical standpoint, its most distinguishing element is that it was the first Winchester lever action fed from an internal box magazine.

This was the first big-boy lever action in history. The Winchester 1886 changed the game because its strong locking-block action was able to handle proper rifle cartridges, rather than the pistol rounds that previous lever action designs were limited to.

It was originally chambered in .45/70 and .45/90, two rounds you can still get it in. Over the years it was loaded for other hard-hitting rounds like the .50/110 Winchester and .33 WCF.

Those rounds, combined with its excellent handling characteristics, made the Model 1886 the first true big-game capable lever action. Today, you can order it in a Saddle Ring Carbine configuration (1,630)witha22-inchbarrel,in“ShortRifle”trim(1,450) with a 24-inch round barrel, or go all out with the fancy Deluxe Case Hardened model ($1,930) with a 24-inch octagonal barrel, upgraded walnut and color case hardened receiver.

Arguably the finest lever action ever (and if there’s one thing lever gun fans like to do its argue about which is best), the Savage Model 99 was a revolutionary addition to the American sporting scene when it was trotted out in 1899.

It had an elegant, hammerless design, used an innovative rotary magazine that allowed the rifle to safely chamber cartridges with spitzer-style pointed bullets, and a stock silhouette that oozed sexiness and speed decades before such aesthetics became the hallmark of art deco industrial design.

First called the Model 1899, it officially changed to the Model 99 in 1921 when the .300 Savage was introduced. Initially, the 1899 was chambered in .303 Savage and .30/30 Win. Soon, Savage added other cartridges to the lineup—the most iconic of which was Charles Newton’s speedster, the .250-3000 Savage, in 1915. Later in life, the Model 99 added the .243 Win., .308 Win., 7mm-08 Rem., .375 Win. and others to the mix.

My Model 99 is a particularly lovely rifle. It was given to me by my father-in-law before he passed away and is a takedown model chambered in .300 Savage that includes a .410 bore barrel that it shoots single-shot.

The rifle was sold by Abercrombie and Fitch to legendary car maker Carroll Shelby, who eventually gave it to my father-in-law as a gift. It’s still in its original case of leather and wood lined with purple velvet. I rarely shoot it—but admire it frequently.

Though it never gained the following of the Savage 99, the Winchester Model 88 is similar to the Savage in that it incorporated a lot of technical innovation in its design and caused hunters and shooters to reassess the lever action platform.

Winchester unveiled it in 1955. It had a short lever throw and used a rotating three-lug bolt that smoothly stripped rounds from the detachable box magazine. The Model 88 was chambered in a handful of cartridges that were new at the time, specifically the .308 Win., .243 Win., .284 Win. and the .358 Win., which was a particularly terrific brush round that is sadly all but forgotten these days.

The Model 88 has a hammerless design and side eject, which allows for easy mounting of an optic on the receiver. One particularly clever feature is how the trigger moves with the lever loop, eliminating the possibility of a pinched finger or snagged glove when working the action.

I don’t think there’s a rimfire lever action as beloved as the Marlin 39A. It tops many shooters’ lists as the best .22 LR ever produced. The legacy of the 39A is fascinating. It started as the Model 1891 and was the first .22 LR lever action produced. Its legendary accuracy was demonstrated by Annie Oakley who used one in her shooting exhibitions. The Model 39A held the distinction of being the longest continually produced shoulder-fired firearm in history. That streak was broken when the dimwits who purchased Marlin and placed it under the Remington umbrella decided to move Marlin’s production facilities from North Haven, Conn., to Ilion, New York—at which point the production of all Marlins ground to a (predictable) halt.

My sincere hope is that we’ll soon—as in the next couple years—be able to reclassify the 39A under the “Best Lever Action Rifles Being Currently Made” category since it seems Ruger is doing such a fabulous job reviving Marlin since they purchased it.

When you think “cowboys” and the “Old West” the first rifle that comes to mind is this beauty. The Winchester 73 really was the right gun for the right time—being the first rifle chambered for the .44-40, which is said to be the first centerfire cartridge developed. Whether it deserved to be called “The Gun that Won the West” as Winchester touted, there’s no denying that the Model 73 was used to send a whole bunch of men—both good and bad—to their maker, and accounted for innumerable deer and other game to boot.

The Model 1873 was produced until 1923 but has enjoyed a revival since the sport of cowboy action shooting sprang up. Uberti makes replicas chambered in .357 Mag. and .45 Colt, while Winchester, which worked with their Japanese partner Miroku, has been importing ’73s since 2013. Those are available in .357 Mag., .45 Colt, and .44-40 WCF.

Since the barrel of a lever action is longer than that of a handgun, cartridges like the .357 Mag. and .44 Mag. get a significant performance boost in terms of velocity that makes them more capable on animals like deer and hogs.In addition, a lever-action chambered in .357 can run .38 Spl. rounds, which are economical and have little recoil making it a great option for plinking and practice.

Yes. They are fast-handling, quick-shooting, easy to wield and carry, hold good quantities of ammo, are available in a wide range of cartridges for different applications, and are legal in most all jurisdictions. Whether you’re on horseback with one in a scabbard or have a take-down model in a bug-out bag, lever-actions are an excellent choice.

Are lever-actions effective on dinosaurs?

Absolutely. The Marlin 1895 SBL carried by Chris Pratt’s character—dinosaur whisperer Owen Grady—in Jurassic World, would be a top choice as a dino stopper, provided it was loaded with heavy, hard-hitting ammo like Buffalo Bore’s 380-grain mono-metal WFN dangerous-game load.

Certainly. A carbine-length lever action chambered in a pistol cartridge like .357 Mag. or .44 Mag. would be a highly effective option for home protection. Even a rifle chambered in .22 Win. Mag. can be a formidable home-defense gun when loaded with ammo like Federal Punch.

Usually when one compiles a “best of” list—whether talking deer rifles, elk cartridges, or sniper rifles—there is significant push-back with the selections. Everyone has deeply-held convictions on such matters.

With lever action rifles, it is a bit different. There are many rifles that are universally agreed upon. No one in their right mind is going to say that a Savage 99 isn’t one of the best lever action rifles of all time. The same goes for the Model 94, Marlin 336 and others.

I think we rally around lever actions because they are the quintessential American rifle. Yes, we make the best bolt-actions in the world, and the same can be argued with other firearms platforms—but the lever action is distinctly ours. Though some are made abroad and imported, the lever action is, and always will be, America’s rifle.

John B. Snow is Shooting Editor of Outdoor Life, where he oversees the publication’s firearms and shooting coverage. This includes gear reviews, features on technical innovations, stories on shooting techniques and general hunting coverage with the occasional fishing story thrown into the mix.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8282. Day 11 – Pulling the Ripcord

After a long night of contemplation and hard choices, I decided to get off the trail.  I considered continuing to Tan Hill and its famous pub.  However, I believe that Tan Hill is even more remote than Keld.  If I arrived and decided that I needed medical assistance, it would be nearly impossible to arrange.  Additionally, the pub at Tan Hill was completely booked, so I would have to rely on camping on the grounds around the pub.

I would need to find my way to the nearest town and make a plan from there.  Somehow, I still need to get to Kirk Yetholm by my previously-planned arrival date.  I mailed my extra gear to the Border Hotel and I have a two-night reservation.  Graeme and Rachel told me that they will be finishing the Way on that same day.  If I keep to my schedule, I could meet up with them at the end of the Pennine and celebrate their accomplishment.

Two days after that, I need to be in Edinburgh for my scheduled flight home.

After packing up my camp, I walked into the Keld proper.  It was even smaller and more remote than I realized.  Sitting at the Keld Green Café, sipping a cappuccino, I discovered that the nearest town was Kirkby Stephan, about 10 miles away.  There are no buses in Keld.  I’d be looking at a 4 hour walk at best.

I tried using the Uber app, but after an hour of searching, the app literally apologized and gave up.  I tried a taxi app as well and received the same result.  No one was willing to make the drive from Kirkby Stephen.  I talked to the café owner; he suggested I try hitchhiking.

As I sat contemplating my options, I met Richard and Jackie, two people who were walking England’s Coast-to-Coast trail.  That trail intersects the Pennine Way at Keld.  Jackie was not taking my situation lightly.  She got on her phone and started calling taxi companies in Kirkby Stephen.  Before long, she had arranged to have a taxi make the long haul to Keld and back.  It was pricey, but at this point, I was glad to pay it.

It was almost an hour before the cab showed up.  While I waited, Jackie insisted on buying me another cappuccino.  When the driver pulled up, I thanked her profusely, declared to everyone at the café that she was a living angel, and ran for the cab.

On the drive down to Kirkby Stephan, I could see why drivers were reluctant to pick up fares from Keld.  The country road is long, narrow, and winding.  I’m not prone to motion sickness, but this road really pushed my tolerance.  After 40 minutes, we pulled up in front of the Pennine Inn.  I tipped the driver generously and went inside.  The room was lovely, and the staff, even lovelier.  Realizing that I was injured, they went out of their way to help me.  They were absolutely incredible.

Now came the task of figuring out how I was going to get from this inn to Kirk Yetholm in Scotland, nearly 120 miles away.  After hours on my phone, planning, purchasing train tickets, and making hotel reservations, I came up with the following itinerary:

I made all my reservations at hotels and inns within walking distance of the nearest train station.  Many of them were across the street from the station.

The next issue was timing the day of arrival in Kirk Yetholm.  My impression was that this tiny village would not offer a lot of entertainment or distraction.  Getting there too early was not going to be much fun.  Therefore, I decided that I would take a day or two at the end of each travel leg on my schedule.  Be a tourist!  See some of the sites along my route and do my best to enjoy my time in the UK.

And that’s what I did.  I visited towns and cities, toured castles, ate good food, touched the North Sea, and generally just wandered around admiring whatever crossed my path.  Unfortunately, I was still limping, even with the ankle brace, and had to limit my walking distance.  There were occasional bouts of melancholy over my failed attempt at the Pennine.  I felt good about walking nearly 120 miles of the Way, certainly the longest distance I had ever experienced by a very wide margin.  Mostly, I just tried to enjoy my travels.

#8281. New Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health issues. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The new line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

This was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

#8280. An Old-School Perspective on Finding Better Duck Hunting: Get Creative and Target the Hardest Places

Published Oct 27, 2026 3:00 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The way some hunters talk, you’d think good waterfowl hunting was a thing of the past. Sure, it was great 25 years ago. You could pick almost any field or pothole and shoot a limit of ducks. But millions of ducks and geese still sweep the flyways each fall, and a determined hunter can find good shooting. It’s just that you have to hunt the hard places.

That’s my name for spots that teem with ducks and geese but rarely see a hunter. Sometimes these areas demand too much effort, but more often hard places are open expanses that offer a hunter no place to hide. Pastures, the favorite haunts of Canada geese, are one example. How can you blind on a pasture as flat as a billiard table? A flooded field also is a problem. Hunters line the dikes of flooded stubblefields like fence posts, but few of them head for the middle because there’s no place to hide. The potential for open-water hunting on lakes, reservoirs, and bays, where waterfowl raft by the thousands, has hardly been touched. The windswept expanses of open ice where geese frequently rest has great possibilities too. In some parts of the United States a person has little choice about where to hunt. But in many regions, particularly in the prairie and Western states, hard places with excellent hunting abound.

Most hunters credit ducks and geese with too much intelligence. Some waterfowlers would have you believe that the Canada goose, for example, is second cousin to Einstein. That image of brilliance is ridiculous. Geese and other birds are smart just as dogs are smart. To teach a dog to sit, you push his rear down and say, “Sit!” After a few lessons he’ll sit when you give the command. Waterfowl learn similarly. On heavily hunted lands waterfowl avoid cover because they’ve learned that’s where the shots come from.

In much open country they’ve had no such conditioning. No one has shot at them, so ducks fall over themselves to land in decoys placed far from cover. In the hard places, waterfowl aren’t conditioned to be cautious. That is the basis for good bird hunting. It also accounts for the fact that you don’t need much of a blind in the open. Hunting hard places is more a matter of philosophy than of technique. Once you’ve decided to hunt a hard place you’ve cleared a major hurdle. Then you just get out there and start hunting. To show how simple it is, I’ll tell you about some ways my friends and I have hunted the hard places.

I usually don’t use a blind. In my part of Oregon, Canada geese spend a lot of time feeding and resting on pastures, and most ranchers don’t want their sod dug up for blinds. A blind above ground also is about as conspicuous as a high-rise apartment building. The only option is no blind. So you just lie on the ground.

Any hunter knows movement really spooks waterfowl, so being able to disguise yourself as a frozen clump of mud is the big step in making this work. I usually clump a few goose decoys around my body and put one in front of my face. The oversize shell decoys made today are especially good for this kind of hunting. A friend of mine has made silhouette decoys that are so large he can curl up behind one. In late season, when swans are present, I’ve used large swan silhouettes among my duck and goose decoys. This technique has worked especially well on ice, when I’ve worn a white suit and lain behind a swan silhouette.

Put your decoys as far from ditches and weed patches as you can. Set up where birds don’t expect danger. Look for small depressions, places where the grass is lumpy, or pressure ridges on the ice so you can hide. Even a slight variation will make you less obvious. And wear clothing that looks like the ground. The obvious choice after a snowfall would be to wear a white suit or to cover yourself over with a sheet. When the cover is green, pull a square of green camouflage cloth over yourself. Some of the pastures I’ve hunted in are muddy. My hunting coat is so impregnated with dirt it looks like part of the ground, so I often don’t cover myself with anything. An occasional roll in the mud keeps the blind fresh.

On windy days this simple approach is almost foolproof. The birds fly low and come directly in from the downwind side. Obviously you want to lie on the upwind side of a decoy. On calm days when waterfowl fly higher and sometimes circle, it’s not as easy, especially if you gawk at them.

In my region farmers flood their grainfields after harvest. Flooded fields draw ducks the way a candy store draws kids. For years I pondered the featureless expanses of water and mud, trying to figure out how I’d get out there without sinking out of sight forever. Then it struck me—an air mattress. Along with a huge bag of floating decoys, I dragged a well-inflated canvas air mattress into a partly flooded field. With the decoys downwind, I flopped the mattress on a clump of mud and lay on it, face up, and pulled a piece of camouflage cloth over me. Ducks and geese nearly landed on me. An air mattress will do the trick in any soggy spot where you can anchor it to some ground. But don’t try it in deep water.

A rubber raft is best for deep water. I use a two-man, rubberized, olive drab canvas raft. You can find these at big sports stores or surplus stores.

The raft can be dragged or carried to any location, and it often serves where a rigid, heavy duckboat won’t. I’ve used it in the same fields I used to hunt with an air mattress. It also works well in marshes where only a few inches of grass show above the surface of the water. I got this idea from watching a hunter one day in a flooded stubblefield. He had a low-profile boat, which he covered with chicken wire. He tied stubble all over the wire, then crawled under it into the boat. His simple blind looked like a mat of straw lying on the water. Ducks swarmed into his decoys as if he weren’t there.

From that example I made a chicken-wire cover for my raft, with a flap cut out of the middle so I could sit up and have an area to shoot through. I tied short pieces of decoy line on the chicken wire and used these to tie grass, stubble, lily pads, and other appropriate plants to the wire. In addition, I cut a floor for the raft made of 3/8-inch plywood. With some spar varnish for weatherproofing and a strip of outdoor carpet stapled around the floor’s edge to keep it from chafing the raft, I had a rigid bottom that made the raft stable. I can sit, kneel, or stand in it without much wobbling.

Another item that could be used in the same way as the rubber raft is a float tube, or belly boat. While these are made for fishing small waters, they’re well suited to hunting. I recently got one with a camouflage cover, and it looks like part of the marsh. With a chicken-wire cone covered with tules, it would look just like a muskrat house.

If the water is too shallow to use a float tube in the conventional manner—with your legs dangling in the water—you can use it as a shooting platform. One friend, Dave Hummel, did something similar with a tire inner tube. Dave saw lots of pintails on big marsh ponds. Those educated birds weren’t about to land within shooting range of the tule fringes, where a hunter could hide. They stuck to the middle of the huge ponds, where the only cover was a few patches of lily pads that stuck up a few inches above the water. There was no way to blind a boat out there, and a person couldn’t lie down in the foot-deep water. So Dave wired a round piece of plywood to the top of an inner tube. To hunt those smart pintails he threw his decoys onto the open water and put his inner tube table in the lily pads. He laid his gun and shells on the platform and camouflaged it with lily pads. Dressed in chest waders he was able to kneel behind it. To hide from circling ducks, he put his face down on the platform. When ducks were within range, he rose on his knees to shoot. Tough shooting? Yes. But it was the only way to get within range of those ducks, and Dave got his share of them.

I recently fished with a fellow who had a “boat” called a Bass Tracker Bantam. It’s a flat plastic hull about five feet long made for poking around backwaters for bass. It’s very stable and rises no more than six inches from the water. It looks to me like an ideal piece of equipment for hard-place hunting.

Another friend hunted from shallow water by using a piece of heavy brown plastic. The water, matted with weeds, was only three or four inches deep. He laid a 12×12-foot square of plastic on the water and jumped into the middle of it. The weeds held up the edges of the plastic to keep water out and he was able to lie down to hide from ducks without getting wet.

Open water may be the extreme example of a hard place to hunt. These days, with many huge reservoirs next to croplands, lots of ducks and geese rest on wide water. A sink box is the answer, but sink boxes are illegal. The next best thing is a low-profile boat. You can’t hide such a boat so you try to make it look like floating debris. My friend David Hagerbaumer hunts extensively on open bays along the Pacific Coast. He uses a Barnegat sneakbox, a flat boat that looks like a miniature hydroplane. Dave has a net for the boat that camouflages it, and he puts seagull decoys on the decks. On open water the boat just looks like a piece of flotsam drifting on the bay. Dave lies on his back in the boat, facing his decoys, which are downwind. This rig works well on diving ducks, and Dave often takes puddle ducks and brant while hunting from it too.

On an incoming tide, puddle ducks often work the shores of estuaries to feed on the flooding beaches and tidal marshlands. That’s when Dave hunts the edges, and he camouflages his boat by tying grass to the net covering, or by shoveling mud clumps onto the decks.

Dave has another rig, called an alligator, that should really do the job for you on mudflats or beaches. These are no longer available commercially, but you could easily make your own. The alligator is a fiberglass coffin, shaped like a mummy with an oblong hole cut out of one side. You drag it out to where you want to hunt, dig a hole, and bury the thing, except for the opening. Then you crawl in, lie on your back, and face up through the hole. It’s no more than a way to stay dry while hiding in a soggy place, but that’s all you need in the hard places.

Hunting hard places can be a little wet and dirty. A rugged, heavy pair of chest waders and a canvas coat that can withstand abuse are necessities. The right gun also is important. Guns get muddy in hard places, and most autoloaders I’ve used turn into single shots under these conditions. A pump gun is OK because you can grind shells through even if the gun does take on a load of grime, but the best choice is a double barrel, which is nearly impervious to dirt. Invariably in hard places you must shoot lying on your back, sitting, or from your knees. Your feet may be stuck in the mud, and you’ll feel like you’re caught in a spiderweb when you start trying to shoot through a chicken-wire cover. Add to that a good stiff breeze, which ducks can use to get quickly out of range, and you have a shooting challenge. A good idea is to practice shooting claybirds from awkward positions, also lie down and practice throwing your gun to your shoulder and swinging it. You may want to learn to shoot both right and left-handed so you can handle ducks coming in from both sides.

Hard places generally call for big decoy spreads. In open expanses, ducks in particular congregate in huge swarms. I can pile about five dozen inflatable ducks on my rubber raft so that’s about my maximum, but more decoys would be even better.

The last day of the season a couple of years ago typifies hard-place hunting. Ducks were streaming into a flooded stubblefield and hunters lined the dikes around the field. I waded out to the middle, found a small patch of mud to lie on, and threw out some decoys. Mallards broke their necks to get into that spread. But the mud was sticky and the wind was howling. By the time I could sit up to shoot, the ducks usually had flared to long range. The one box of shells in my pocket accounted for only four mallards and a honker. But it was an unforgettable afternoon of duck hunting. While hunters pass-shooting from the dikes only took an occasional high bird, I was at the center of a swarming, teeming mass of ducks.

Read Next: Duck Hunting’s New Reality: It Will Keep Getting Tougher for the Workaday Waterfowler

Great hunting still does exist. It demands some ingenuity and hard work. But if you hunt the hard places, you’ll find the birds. And that’s what duck hunting is all about.

#8277. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#8274. My AT Thru-Hike: By the Numbers

Hey folks, back at it with another post here.  I’ve been meaning to write a recap of my hike pretty much sense I finished hiking the trail back in August, but alas, I am only getting to it now. Now that I am settled firmly into post-trail life, back home and working again, I took the chance to analyze my hike a bit. Compiled below are some interesting or funny insights (at least to me) of my thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail.  Hopefully you will find this insightful if you are planning your own AT thru-hike or at least entertaining…

Here is a complete breakdown of the costs that I incurred while on my At thru-hike.  While I don’t think I was egregious in my spending, I didn’t exactly skimp either.  I could have easily shaved off some expenses, especially in the food department.  However, after long hiking days, I simply enjoyed the comforts provided by cold beverages and warm food!

Right out of the pouch, just like God intended!

Along the trail I saw and experienced much, including wildlife!  The highlight here were the Fishers!  I only got a quick glimpse of both of them, as they are quite elusive creatures, but I will take what I can get!  And while I saw quite a few deer all along the trail, the deer in Shenandoah and the Smokies were shameless!  Often coming right up to my tent at night or in the morning, including one that didn’t even flinch when I popped my head out and was close enough I could have pet it!

This was surprisingly close to Tinker Cliffs in the Virginia Triple Crown area!

For sleeping along the trail I definitely preferred my tent over shelters, and spent a good deal of the trail actively avoiding shelters!  In Maine I softened this stance quite a bit for a few reasons.  The first being that Maine was the rainiest state of my hike, so there was some shelter hopping from one to another in the attempt to keep some of my gear and myself dry.  The second being I was exhausted a lot towards the end and saving a little bit of time and energy by sleeping in the shelter was worth it.  And finally, towards the end I just couldn’t bother to care about mice running around me at night that much.  Plus, the rest of the Board (Shooter and Birdie) was doing it!

First night on trail at Hidden Pond during the March Megastorm. I met friends that I would keep through the end of the trail. Especially Shooter, Queso, Zipper, and Beer Run!

Here are some fun and random stats from my hike.  These add some color to the story of my hike. Like falling 10ft off a dam, cutting your leg open, and needing to get stitches!

#8273. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Plan B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team said that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet

There was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

Nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

#8270. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#8267. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

While they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

Locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Company

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Company officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8264. Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

“Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

The ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

The climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below shows that the new French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the new route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain

Meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

“It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”

But this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni

#8261. Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

Caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

The pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

With no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

The paddling portion went quickly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”

Using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They also effectively halved the 480km trek by packrafting over two large lakes, including Nettilling, the world’s largest lake on an island. Yet there was no way to ease the final 160km slog into Iqaluit.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they said.

McDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

“One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We quickly packed our boats and got on the water.”

In Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8259. The 9 Ways That Mature Bucks Are Different Than Other Deer

Published Oct 27, 2026 4:29 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Almost every deer on the farm is on its feet. Bucks and does of all ages are hammering food sources. They’re hungry after the rut, but there’s also a snowstorm incoming. Temps are dropping, and there’s a flurry of snowfall — and activity.

Even though the entire herd appears to be on its feet, one buck is still holed up in his fortress. It’s broad daylight, frigid, and snowing. The 5-year-old you want to kill refuses to leave his bedding sanctuary. He’ll move in daylight — all deer must move eventually — but not until it gets closer to dark.

It’s been said many times, but a deer and a mature buck are two different animals.  Older bucks don’t just have more inches of antler on average — they have more wits, senses, and experience. You don’t get to be a five-year-old deer without learning how to survive in the wild, and that’s why these deer not only look different but behave in ways that don’t often align with the does and younger bucks we’re used to seeing. Here’s how.

Hunters can use many physical signs to estimate a buck’s age, but the key I often look for is a buck’s muscle definition. Older whitetails look vastly different than their younger cohorts. Mature bucks have a muscled-up body structure that younger deer just don’t have. As deer progress through each age bracket, they exhibit different body structures.

For example, yearling bucks look like small does with antlers. Two-year-old bucks look like large does with antlers. Three-year-old bucks exhibit a more muscular frame but aren’t filled out just yet. Four-year-old bucks show significant swelling, with heavy shoulders and an enlarged brisket and neck. Five-year-old bucks and older exhibit even more body weight with heavy swelling of the neck, shoulders, and brisket. They might even begin displaying a pot belly and swayed back. Practice judging age in the field, and you’ll be able to better recognize an old buck when he shows up.

Every set of antlers is unique, regardless of the buck’s age. Still, as bucks reach older age classes, they express their genetic code and capabilities. Often, this leads to antler character traits that are usually present in older deer, regardless of the overall score or size of a deer. Examples include kickers, stickers, drop tines, and other unique antler points. It can even lead to greater numbers of points and other interesting non-typical characteristics. Even as they age and their antler size may decrease, older deer still tend to have more mass than younger bucks, particularly around the bases of their antlers.

Deer don’t have personalities in the human sense, but researchers have identified behavioral preferences that we can think of as personalities — particularly when it comes to their movements across the landscape. Some bucks are homebodies or wanderers. (One study found that 33 percent of bucks had a mobile personality.) And as bucks reach older age classes, these personalities can become even more apparent. For example, bucks might be more aggressive or passive. They might be more or less engaged in the rut. Perhaps they even express preferences for specific food sources. If you can start to identify those tendencies and preferences, you have a better shot of patterning your buck.

A common myth suggests that bucks increase their home ranges as they age. For the vast majority of whitetails, this isn’t true. Numerous studies have determined that whitetail buck home ranges and core areas actually decrease in size as they get older. As they become more familiar with their surroundings, they learn the safest areas, best bedding, premier food sources, and more. This leads to a more distinct and deliberate use of the landscape. Hunting older bucks requires finding these smaller areas and home ranges and hunting them accordingly.

As bucks get older, they become more in tune with their environment. They learn where hunters focus their efforts (we humans can become patternable and predictable) and how to avoid us. Older bucks use the landscape to their advantage, especially from a safety perspective.

For instance, bucks use thermal hubs, the low points in the topography where scent collects from the surrounding area. In other words, they don’t necessarily have to walk just downwind of your stand to know there’s a hunter in the area.

Another example includes bucks bedding in ways that give them a security advantage. For instance, mature bucks often bed on leeward ridges, ridge endings, bench edges, and more. Bedding in certain ways allows them to see danger coming from a distance while also smelling any threats upwind that could approach from behind them.

Bucks are also good at finding trails and travel routes that elude stand locations, blinds, and other hunting setups.

Let’s dig even deeper into a buck’s bedding habits, all of which are proven methods that help mature deer detect danger before it detects them. From a scenting perspective, deer find many ways to benefit from prevailing winds and daily thermals.

Using Advantageous Terrain: Bucks tend to bed in areas with advantageous terrain. These locations give them better visibility but also provide winding advantages. As noted above, hilly and mountainous terrain allows deer to use topography to their advantage, but even flatland whitetails find ways to do this. Often, deer that bed in flatter creek or river bottomlands bed close to the water.

For example, deer routinely bed in oxbows. A location with water on three sides helps diminish the odds of a predator approaching from those directions. And if they do, deer can hear them coming through the water. Meanwhile, they can see danger that comes by way of land. If something does approach, deer can bolt out the back door and across the water to safety.

As mentioned above, bucks tend to express a unique personality type. Within those individual preferences comes varied responses to hunting pressure. Human intrusion impacts every deer differently, but most mature bucks don’t tolerate much of it. If they do, they’ve likely been conditioned to certain activities on the property. In other words, some mature bucks may tolerate more pressure than others, but in general, mature bucks won’t tolerate all of it.

Though all bucks are biologically motivated to participate in the rut, some individual bucks can be more active than others. Depending on an individual buck’s tendencies, they might be very active and move a lot during daylight, or they might be reclusive, searching for does at night and bedding back down before daylight.

Read Next: Best Hunting Rifles, Tested and Reviewed

Numerous expert hunters I’ve talked to agree on one particular thing — bucks are hardest to hunt from ages four to six. Often when a buck hits seven, eight, or older, they seem to become more active during the daylight. Perhaps they become overconfident, get delusional and senile, or maybe they just care less. Regardless, they move more and get easier to kill again, almost as a 3-year-old buck would.

Hunting old bucks requires different approaches and tactics than hunting deer in general (does and younger bucks). So, put together a good plan this season, and tag that old buck that’s been haunting your dreams.
