#8161. The Best Survival Food, Tested and Reviewed

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Regarding survival, a reliable food supply is high on the list of needs for disaster readiness. A well-rounded, easy-to-transport kit that keeps you nourished for days—without repeating the same bland meals—is crucial for morale and sustenance.

Many survival food companies are on the market, but not all have stood the test of time. Over the years, several have failed due to poor quality control and mismanagement. As a disaster readiness and survival training professional, I receive samples from many of these companies and, more importantly, have the unique opportunity to have hundreds of students test their products yearly. Additionally, I bring these samples to our courses to gather feedback from our instructors and participants. The insights shared in this article are based on decades of personal experience and the collective input of our students, providing you with a well-rounded perspective to help you make informed decisions about your food preparedness.

At the end of the day, no matter the crisis, we all need food to keep us going. While it’s true that humans can survive for weeks without eating, very few would willingly test that theory. The good news is that with the growing demand, more high-quality, nutrient-dense options are now available. After testing some of the best survival food on the market, these are our top picks for flavor, shelf life, and nutrition.

4Patriots has established itself as one of the leading survival food brands in the market. Proudly made and packaged in the United States, their products support local businesses while delivering high-quality meals. These meals are crafted for superior nutrition and taste, using fresh ingredients and whole grains, and are free from MSG. Preparation is simple—boil water, add the pouch, and within 15 minutes, you’ll have a hot meal ready to eat.

4Patriots packages their food in triple-layer Mylar to ensure long shelf life, which helps protect the contents from air and moisture. Customers can select from various kit sizes depending on their needs, from 72-hour emergency supplies to year-long provisions. Each kit is designed to provide one person with six servings a day, offering sufficient calories and nutrients to sustain energy. The meals come in various flavors, including macaroni and cheese, vegetable soup, and oatmeal. One of my favorite pieces of their kits is that many of the meals are named after people to add some morale build into it all.  No matter the kit size, 4Patriots offers a reliable solution for building a robust survival food supply.

A vital feature of an MRE is the built-in heater, which, once activated, heats your entrée, providing the convenience of a hot meal no matter where you are. However, there are some notable downsides. Many of our students, particularly those with military experience who have relied on MREs for extended periods, advise against using them for long-term situations. In addition to being heavy to transport, they can lead to digestive problems, ranging from constipation to more organ-related severe issues over time.

Providing a hot meal for your family during a disaster is more than just a practical necessity—it can help boost morale and alleviate anxiety, offering a sense of normalcy amidst the chaos. Mountain House meals taste delicious and require boiling water for preparation. Mountain House is a regular staple of meal choices in our classes. I see them often.

One of the great features is that the food rehydrates directly in the pouch, allowing you to eat from it, which means minimal cleanup afterward. With nearly 30 meal options, including breakfasts and desserts, variety won’t be an issue, and no one will find the meals repetitive.

Each serving offers about 250 calories, depending on the meal. With two servings per pouch, there’s plenty for even a hearty appetite or enough to share if needed. These meals are designed to stay fresh for up to 30 years and ensure you can access quality food for decades.

Crafted with Whey Protein Isolate as the primary protein source and fortified with high fiber while containing just 1 gram of sugar, these protein bars are perfect for daily enjoyment. Each Kirkland Signature bar offers 21 grams of high-quality protein and features real chocolate for a satisfying blend of taste and nutrition. Typically used for meal replacement and workout-focused diets, these bars conveniently meet your protein and fiber needs without compromising flavor.

In the context of disaster preparedness, these protein bars are an ideal addition to any emergency food supply. Their long shelf life, combined with their nutritional profile, makes them an excellent option for staying energized and nourished when fresh food may not be available. Lightweight and easy to store, they offer a reliable source of protein and fiber that can help maintain energy levels and support overall health during a crisis. Whether sheltering in place or on the move, these bars ensure access to essential nutrients in challenging circumstances.

Augason Farms is renowned for its extensive line of canned goods, which are perfect for long-term food storage and emergency preparedness. Their #10 cans are filled with freeze-dried or dehydrated foods, offering various essentials, such as fruits, vegetables, meats, grains, and dairy products. With a shelf life of up to 25 years, these canned goods are an excellent choice for those looking to build a reliable food supply for emergencies or everyday convenience. Each can is sealed for freshness and labeled with detailed preparation instructions, making incorporating these products into daily meals or survival situations easy.

Augason Farms’ canned goods are appealing because of their versatility and nutritional value. Whether you need individual ingredients like powdered eggs, instant potatoes, or freeze-dried strawberries, their products allow for flexibility in meal planning. You can use them in recipes or enjoy them independently, ensuring you have access to nutritious food options when fresh ingredients are unavailable. These canned goods are compact, easy to store, and offer large quantities, making them ideal for families, survivalists, or anyone seeking to stock up on essential food supplies that can withstand the test of time.

Peak Refuel is a top choice for disaster preparedness, offering high-protein, freeze-dried meals designed to keep you fueled during challenging situations. Maintaining strength and energy is essential in emergencies, and Peak Refuel meals deliver an impressive 40-50 grams of protein per serving. This high protein content ensures you get the nutrition needed to stay alert and physically capable when it matters most. Whether you’re sheltering in place or need to be on the move, these meals provide the sustenance required to get through physically demanding conditions.

Beyond their nutritional value, Peak Refuel meals are incredibly convenient for disaster preparedness. Made with high-quality, non-GMO ingredients, they rehydrate quickly with hot water and are ready to eat in minutes. The lightweight, resealable pouches are easy to store and transport, making them an ideal addition to any emergency food supply. Various meal options, including breakfast scrambles and hearty dinners like chicken alfredo or beef stroganoff, offer the nutrients you need and great taste to keep morale high during tough times. Peak Refuel’s focus on protein-rich, easy-to-prepare meals makes them an excellent choice for anyone serious about disaster readiness.

ReadyWise is a leading provider of long-term food storage solutions, offering various affordable, high-quality meals that are perfect for disaster preparedness. Whether you’re planning for a short-term emergency or looking to build a comprehensive survival food stockpile, ReadyWise provides convenient, easy-to-prepare options. Their freeze-dried meals only require water, making them ideal for emergencies or outdoor adventures where resources may be limited. With a focus on both taste and nutrition, ReadyWise ensures that their products not only sustain you during a crisis but also offer flavors you can enjoy.

One of the standout features of ReadyWise is its budget-friendly approach, making it a top choice for those who want to prepare without breaking the bank. Despite the lower price point, ReadyWise doesn’t compromise on quality or variety, offering satisfying and nutritionally balanced meals. This combination of affordability and convenience makes ReadyWise a smart investment for families and individuals looking to secure a reliable food supply for potential emergencies. With ReadyWise, you can build your preparedness plan without overspending, ensuring peace of mind for whatever the future holds.

To select the foods we tested, we received samples from a variety of reputable companies and also purchased additional products to ensure a wide range of options. With the help of our students, who have diverse tastes and preferences, we got a broad spectrum of feedback during the testing process. These foods were integrated directly into our survival and disaster readiness training courses, allowing us to evaluate their practicality, taste, and ease of preparation in real-world scenarios. This hands-on approach ensured that we tested the food’s quality and performance under survival conditions.

A structured approach to survival prioritization is best understood through the “Law of Threes” hierarchy. This principle outlines that our most immediate needs, in order of importance, are safety, thermoregulation, hydration, and finally, food. However, from a psychological and moral standpoint, food remains a constant desire, even though it ranks lower on essential needs.

We also took a multi-tiered approach to assessing these survival food options.  I am fond of saying that “hunger is the best seasoning in the world.”  That is true in the long term, but taste plays a role in the short term.  When assessing them, I emphasize both taste and cost-effectiveness. After all, it makes little sense to invest in provisions that are not enjoyable to eat. In addition to these factors, I consider the following critical criteria in my recommendations:

One of the most overlooked factors when choosing survival food is whether or not you enjoy eating it. Taste, texture, and how the food agrees with your digestive system are essential. While it’s easy to focus on stockpiling a large quantity of food, if you don’t like it, you’re essentially wasting money. Some may argue that you’ll eat anything in extreme hunger, but right now, you have the luxury of selecting food you’ll enjoy. Regularly incorporating these meals into your current diet helps rotate stock and prepares your taste buds for when disaster strikes. As the saying goes, “We do not rise to the occasion; we default to our level of training.” Why not start training your palate now?

Cost is another critical consideration when building a survival food supply. Most people must budget carefully, so simultaneously making large purchases may be impossible. A gradual approach works well for many, where small amounts are bought over time as the budget allows. This makes the process more manageable and helps you steadily grow your stockpile without straining your finances. If you face resistance from family members about spending on survival food, consider framing it as an insurance policy—something you invest in for peace of mind in case of a worst-case scenario.

Storage space can be a real challenge for those living in smaller spaces like apartments, condos, or tiny homes. It’s crucial to make the most of your space by considering the size of the packaging and the number of servings per product. This ensures you get the most food stored in the least space. Carefully evaluating your storage setup and choosing compact, efficient products can help maximize your shelf space and investment.

Storing survival food is best done in conditions that are dark, cool, and dry. These three factors will work together to slow down the degradation of the food. A closet in a spare bedroom, for example, might be a great location. A damp basement, perhaps not so much.

Most survival situations tend to last around 72 hours. However, in recent years, many emergencies have extended beyond that timeframe, and with global uncertainty, the possibility of more prolonged events is not just possible but increasingly likely. As a precaution, I recommend planning for at least one month’s worth of food for everyone in your household, ensuring you’re prepared for longer-term scenarios.

As previously mentioned, our primary needs follow a specific order: safety, thermoregulation, water, and food. For safety, ensure you have the tools necessary to protect yourself from both environmental threats and potential harm from others. This includes items to help you see in low-light situations and defend yourself if needed. Thermoregulation involves staying warm in cold weather and cool in hot conditions, so be sure to have adequate clothing and supplies to maintain comfort for at least one month without access to utilities.Water is an invaluable resource, and it’s crucial to have both filtration and purification methods to protect against bacterial and viral contaminants. In addition to these essentials, it’s wise to have signaling tools like bright-colored items, flashlights, and whistles to help attract attention if necessary.

Choosing survival food to keep on hand for emergencies requires a little homework and research. You shouldn’t buy several cases of something simply because the package looks enticing. Base your decision on facts, including budget and the quality of the food. Ease of preparation is also a factor, of course. In an emergency, you may not have ready access to things like stovetops or microwave ovens. Stick with things that require a minimal amount of preparation. Hopefully, you’ll never be in a situation where you must rely on survival food, but you’ll be glad you have it should the unthinkable occur.

Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

#8160. We Tested the Viral ‘Slither Rig’ So You Don’t Have To

Published Nov 5, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

When it comes to bass fishing baits, the Slither Rig is the latest craze on social media. Half flipping bait, half saltwater spoon, this setup certainly raises an eyebrow at first glance. But when an urchin is the most effective lure for catching a bass, who’s to say a saltwater spoon couldn’t work, too? So I set out to try this new contraption, and here’s what I found.

The Slither Rig consists of three parts: a saltwater jigging spoon, a flipping hook, and a flipping bait. Any saltwater jigging spoon will do; I picked up a pack of five for about 12 bucks on Amazon. You’ll want the spoon to weigh at least an ounce, because you’ll essentially be using it as a flipping weight. Remove the hooks from the spoon and replace the back one with a 4/0 flipping hook. Then slide your soft-plastic bait onto the hook, rig it weedless, and you’re ready to go.

The idea behind the Slither Rig is that you replace the traditional bullet-style weight with a spoon and use the weight of that spoon to plunge your bait through thick vegetation. For this style of fishing, you’ll need an extra-heavy/fast flipping/punching rod that’s at least 7 feet, 8 inches long. Pair that rod with a reel with a 7:1 or higher gear ratio, and spool the combo with 65-pound or stronger braid.

I fished the Slither Rig intermittently over the course of three trips, totaling six or seven hours with it. Toward the end of my testing, I finally got a couple of bites flipping thick gator grass and hyacinth mats. But up until that point, I found the Slither Rig to be more trouble than it was worth.

My biggest frustration with the Slither Rig was its inability to punch cleanly through the mat. Granted, I was only using a 1-ounce spoon in areas where I would typically use a 1 1/2-ounce tungsten weight. But this chunk of metal was already as long as my bait, so I didn’t want to go any bigger for fear of increasing the risk of a fish hitting the spoon and missing the bait carrying the hook. And I’m not sure it would have mattered anyway. The issue had less to do with the weight of the setup and more to do with the way it hinged in the middle.

Nine times out of ten, when I flipped the Slither Rig out, it would land flat on the cover and then bend in the middle, causing both the bait and the spoon to catch on the cover. It was like trying to push an already-sprung drywall anchor into a hole in the wall. The physics just didn’t work.

I found that I could flip the bait higher and get it to go through a little better, but the kerplunk of it smacking the mat was off-putting to me and no doubt disturbing to any bass sitting in the foot or two of water beneath the mats. So I was left with no option but to flip the bait onto the mat and then gently jiggle it until it fell through, which worked about a third of the time.

Personally, I don’t see a situation in which the Slither Rig would ever be a better choice than a traditional punching setup. Yes, the spoon adds flash that could have some appeal in stained water, perhaps. But silver tungsten weights can do the same thing, and they punch through cover far more cleanly.

While I did manage to get a couple of bites on the Slither Rig, I have zero doubt that I could have caught more fish had I flipped a traditional pegged punching rig or Texas rig through all of the same areas, simply because I would have been able to present my bait to the bass better.

Is the Slither Rig legit? Practically speaking, no. You may see someone on facespace talking about how it’s the next big thing, but don’t let them fool you. While I did prove to myself that I could get bit on it, the mechanics of the setup just aren’t conducive to heavy cover. Consider this one debunked.

#8159. The 3 Best Ways to Cook a Venison Backstrap

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I ate a lot of venison when I was a kid. Any recipe that could be made with beef, my mother made with deer meat — hamburgers, spaghetti sauce, pot roast, and more. However, she didn’t ever get too creative with venison backstraps. Although she realized they were a prized piece of meat, she mostly over-cooked them in a frying pan and then smothered them with gravy.

When I started harvesting my own deer, it felt like preparing a delicious meal was the best way to honor the animal. WIth a little culinary research and some experimentation in the kitchen, I learned that there are far tastier venison backstrap recipes for turning this prime cut into a meal. Here are some of my favorite ways to prepare a venison backstrap. These recipes were refined with whitetail meat, but they also work well for any big game animal.

The backstrap is a super lean and tender strip of meat that runs along a deer’s spine, stretching from the shoulder blades to the last vertebra. There are two backstraps, one on each side of the spine. Each one will weigh 1 to 3 pounds depending on the size of the deer.

The backstrap of a deer is equivalent to ribeye and filet mignon cuts from cattle. However, venison backstraps are much leaner than beef ribeye. It is a coveted cut of meat best served medium rare (between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit). When cooked to a higher temp than that, the meat quickly turns from tender and juicy to dry and chewy.

When it comes off the deer, the backstrap is covered in a layer of connective tissue often referred to as “silver skin.” When exposed to heat, the silver skin becomes very tough. Remove the silver skin before cooking. Here’s how:

Because backstrap is such an inherently delicious and tender cut of meat, it doesn’t really need any elaborate preparations. Sometimes simple is better. It lets the natural taste really shine through. You could even serve just the steaks alone without the mushrooms and onions.

You can really fancy-fy your venison backstrap recipe with this twist on traditional Wellington. The process is long, but the rewards are well worth the effort. Serve with roasted potatoes and winter veggies.This recipe is relatively complicated and has lots of steps. If it seems confusing, check out this step-by-step guide to beef Wellington by Gordon Ramsey. We’re essentially doing the same thing—but with venison and without the accent.

The key to any delicious venison backstrap recipe is to not overcook. Although the loin is naturally tender and juicy, it can turn tough and dry in a hurry with too much exposure to heat. The best venison backstrap will still be plenty pink in the middle.

#8158. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 33-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8157. My Ski Helmet Looks Perfectly Fine. Here’s Why I’m Replacing It Anyway.

Last February, on the final day of SKI’s annual ski test, I caught an edge in variable snow conditions while testing carving skis. I went, as we say, over the handlebars, landing directly on top of my head and compressing my neck.

I knew I’d hit my head, but at the time, I didn’t think much of it. It wasn’t until the following day that I began to understand how hard I’d actually hit the snow.

A few days later, I was sitting in my doctor’s office being diagnosed with a concussion and a neck injury. For months afterward, I dealt with headaches, neck pain, and sensitivity to light and sound. Some nights I’d wake up at 3 or 4 a.m. with pain radiating from the base of my skull, unable to get comfortable enough to fall back asleep. The hardest part was how unpredictable it all felt. I’d think I was getting better, only to have the symptoms flare up again.

The good news? I was wearing a helmet that may have spared me a much more serious head injury. The bad news? Now I have to throw that helmet away.

If I hadn’t developed concussion symptoms, I probably wouldn’t have thought twice about wearing it again. My helmet was brand new, and from the outside, there’s no obvious damage. But apparently, that says little about what’s going on underneath.

Needing a little extra convincing to toss out what looks like a perfectly good, well-fitting helmet, I turned to Madelen Fahlstedt, Ph.D., a biomechanical specialist at MIPS, a helmet-safety technology company. Fahlstedt holds a doctorate in medical engineering from Sweden’s KTH Royal Institute of Technology, where she researched head-injury biomechanics and accident reconstruction.

She explains that most ski helmets contain a layer of expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam designed to absorb impact energy by compressing or deforming. Once it takes a serious hit, that deformation is permanent, meaning the affected foam can’t absorb the same energy again.

“The outer shell can hide these deformations in the EPS. Even from the inside of the helmet, the deformations can be hard to detect,” Fahlstedt says. “To that sense, a helmet is essentially a one-hit-wonder.”

Traditional ski helmets are designed primarily to absorb the energy of an impact, particularly the forces associated with linear motion, when your head strikes something and comes to an abrupt stop. These forces can cause serious injuries, including skull fractures.

But real-world ski crashes aren’t always so straightforward.

When your head hits the snow at an angle, it can also rotate suddenly. That rotational motion can cause different parts of the brain to move relative to one another, stretching delicate tissues.

“The brain is typically more sensitive to rotational motion than linear motion because it has shear properties similar to water or gel,” Fahlstedt explains.

Both linear and rotational forces can contribute to brain injuries, which is why some helmet manufacturers have introduced technologies designed to address rotational motion.

MIPS, for example, doesn’t manufacture helmets. Rather, it develops safety technology that manufacturers can incorporate into their designs. So you might find a MIPS system inside a Smith helmet or a Giro helmet, even though the two models look, fit, and function differently.

Its best-known technology allows a layer inside the helmet to move about 10 to 15 millimeters during certain angled impacts. That small amount of movement is designed to reduce the rotational motion transferred to your head. Depending on the helmet, the layer might be visible or built into the padding.

MIPS is just one approach, however, and no technology can guarantee protection against concussion.

In fact, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is clear that no helmet is concussion-proof. Still, helmets provide meaningful protection. According to a 2022 review by the American Academy of Pediatrics, skiers and snowboarders who wear helmets have roughly 34 percent lower odds of suffering a head injury than those who don’t.

According to Fahlstedt, a helmet should be replaced after a significant impact, regardless of whether there’s visible damage.

The challenge, of course, is figuring out what counts as significant.

A helmet that rolls off a tailgate or gets knocked against the chairlift safety bar isn’t necessarily in the same category as one that absorbs the force of your head hitting hardpack. But a crash doesn’t have to look or feel dramatic to involve substantial forces.

Mine certainly didn’t. Without the concussion diagnosis, I’m not sure I would have considered it a significant impact at all. But as the CDC notes, concussion symptoms can take hours or even days to appear, so how you feel immediately after a crash isn’t necessarily a reliable indicator of injury. If you suspect a concussion, stop skiing and seek medical evaluation.

The same cautious approach applies to your helmet. When in doubt, err on the side of caution. Based on Fahlstedt’s advice and helmet manufacturer guidance, here’s when to replace your ski helmet and what to look for when buying a new one:

These standards establish minimum safety requirements, but they don’t tell you how one helmet compares with another. For that, Fahlstedt points to Virginia Tech’s Snow Sport Helmet Ratings, one of the most respected independent resources for comparing helmet safety.

Its ratings include 56 snowsports helmets and evaluate their performance in laboratory tests measuring both linear and rotational head motion. Rather than simply passing or failing a safety test, helmets receive a one- to five-star rating, giving skiers another way to compare their options. You can compare those ratings with SKI’s 2027 Winter Gear Guide, where we selected the eight best ski helmets for resort and backcountry skiing from 36 models we tested. Our hands-on testing evaluates factors like fit, comfort, ventilation, and usability on the mountain.

It’s tempting to look at nearly new gear, especially something that wasn’t cheap, and convince yourself it’s probably fine. But a helmet isn’t like a scratched pair of goggles or a jacket with a torn sleeve that can make it through another season with a little duct tape.

Mine has already done its job once. I’m not asking it to do it again.

#8156. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

#8155. The Top 30 Ski Resorts in the West (2027)

Choosing a ski resort for your next trip is about more than snow totals and vertical drop. Sure, you want great snow, lifts that keep you moving, and terrain that makes you want to take one more lap. But last winter reminded us just how much conditions can shape a ski experience—and how difficult it can be to judge a resort when much of its terrain isn’t open or skiing the way it should. A lean snow year across much of the West made for a challenging season, and those conditions appear to have left their mark on this year’s rankings, even at some of North America’s most celebrated destinations.

Every spring, we ask readers to weigh in on the resorts they’ve visited, rating their experiences across 18 categories that span the full spectrum of a ski vacation. From snow, grooming, lifts, and terrain variety to dining, lodging, nightlife, and overall character, these rankings reflect the collective wisdom of skiers who’ve experienced these places firsthand. But this year’s results come with an added wrinkle: When terrain is limited and conditions are far from ideal, it’s not always easy to separate a resort’s inherent strengths from the circumstances of the season. The latest survey went out last April, and the results are in.

More Results: Looking For the East Rankings? Click Here.

The 2027 West rankings, below, reveal which resorts are getting the most right, where they truly shine, and where there’s room to improve. Some familiar names took significant tumbles. Others weathered the challenges and climbed higher. These shifts suggest that even resorts with exceptional terrain, amenities, and reputations aren’t immune to a difficult winter. At the same time, these are overall vacation-experience rankings, not a referendum on snow alone. Our reviews break down each resort’s biggest strengths and weaknesses—on and off the slopes—to help you figure out which destination best fits what you’re looking for in a ski trip.

Think of this as advice from your fellow skiers, informed by a winter that didn’t always make for easy comparisons. These rankings aren’t a one-size-fits-all verdict on where you should spend your winter vacation, nor do they tell the whole story of what a resort can deliver in a better snow year. Explore the rankings, see how your favorites stack up, and discover a few places that might deserve a spot on your list. And if you disagree with the results, even better. The Reader Resort Survey returns next spring, giving you another chance to weigh in and help shape next year’s Resort Guide.

New this season, SKI is partnering with Outside Travel to provide seamless hotel-booking options at many of the Top 50 resorts. Navigate to the resort’s personalized landing page next to the “Book Now” bullet to explore lodging by budget and/or location. More destinations are coming online soon, plus revisit for dining and après recommendations from the SKI editors. Join Outside+ for up to 10% off lodging rates.

Big-mountain skiing meets a bona fide ski town, with enough terrain, dining, nightlife, and family-friendly diversions to keep everyone happy—if you can navigate the crowds.

Don’t let Park City’s No. 30 ranking fool you: This resort has a lot going for it. Readers praise its sheer size, varied terrain, and off-mountain amenities, making it one of the West’s most well-rounded destinations for groups with different abilities and interests. With more than 7,300 acres of lift-served terrain, there’s room for just about everyone, from families cruising groomers and exploring beginner-friendly zones to experts hunting steep, gladed pitches like Condor Woods and the high-alpine bowls of McConkey’s.

Then there’s the town itself. Historic Main Street is the real deal, packed with restaurants, bars, shops, and places to stay, while the broader resort scene offers plenty to do long after the lifts close. Park City scores among the best in nightlife, après, dining, and lodging, and readers appreciate that non-skiers can have a vacation here, too. Families also give the destination high marks, thanks to its mix of terrain and off-slope activities. “I love how close the resort is to town and all the restaurants and other amenities,” commented one survey respondent.

Access is another major advantage. Salt Lake City International Airport is close enough that visitors can often land and be skiing within hours, making Park City an easy choice for a long weekend or a family trip. “It’s the easiest large resort to get to in the U.S. with an incredible amount of terrain,” said one SKI reader. But that convenience is a double-edged sword: Crowds can clog base areas and lift lines, while parking headaches and high prices leave readers wishing the overall experience were a better value. Lift bottlenecks remain a particular sore spot, but lift network upgrades coming for the 2027-’28 season hope to move the needle.

This season brings significant upgrades at Canyons Village, including a new enclosed gondola to replace the aging Cabriolet and a five-story parking garage. Those changes should improve the arrival experience, though new parking fees will add another cost for some visitors. Through it all, Park City’s appeal is undeniable: enormous terrain, a lively town, and easy access from a major airport. “It’s a big mountain with lots of options,” said one Park City skier. “Fun and varied terrain and (usually) great snow.”

“Good for both hard-chargers and solid intermediates.  Lots of varied terrain.  Easy to navigate without taking a lot of lifts.”

At Canyons Village, a new enclosed 10-passenger Skyway Gondola replaces the open-air Cabriolet, with a mid-station serving nearby developments and a five-story garage is expected to open in early December with $29 per day (free after noon and for carpools of four-plus).

On the events front, Shaun White’s The Snow League comes to the mountain Jan. 21–23, 2027, bringing elite halfpipe snowboarding and freeskiing competition, live music, and fan events. Park City has rebuilt its 22-foot Eagle Superpipe for the competition, and the pipe will open to the public after the event.

Jaw-dropping Lake Tahoe views, sprawling terrain, and a lively après scene make Heavenly as much about the good times off the slopes as the skiing itself.

At Heavenly, the scenery is almost as memorable as the skiing. Perched above Lake Tahoe, with terrain straddling the California-Nevada border, the resort delivers one spectacular lake view after another across 5,000 acres of skiable terrain. There’s plenty for a range of abilities, from mellow groomers for families and newer skiers to wide-open blues and approachable black diamonds. Even longtime locals can’t resist pausing to take in the view. “I’ve lived in the area for almost 20 years and those lake views still almost knock me off my skis,” confessed one Heavenly fan.

Heavenly earns high marks for nightlife, dining, and lodging, with stellar après spots, craft breweries, and live music around South Lake Tahoe, plus the casinos and entertainment of nearby Stateline, Nevada. Whether you’re looking to keep the party going or settle in for a long dinner after a day on the mountain, there’s plenty to do beyond skiing.

The biggest frustration? Getting around. Readers dinged Heavenly for crowded lifts, including the gondola, and guest service remains an area for improvement. Some base-area facilities could also use a refresh. Still, those complaints have a way of fading when you crest a ridge, turn a corner, and find Lake Tahoe stretched out below you in all its glory. “There’s no shortage of beautiful runs—especially when the sun is shining and the lake is visible from anywhere on top of the mountain.”

“Heavenly has great grooming systems, so no matter how bad the snow gets, the groomers are fun to ride.”

A family-friendly favorite with forgiving groomers, surprisingly adventurous corners, and one of the easiest getaways from Denver.

As the closest major Epic Pass resort to Denver, Keystone draws plenty of Front Range locals alongside visitors looking for a full mountain vacation. The good news is that both are on tap at this family favorite. The frontside can get busy, particularly on weekends, but there’s more to Keystone than its popular cruisers. Head farther out to explore The Outback or venture into Bergman Bowl, where high-alpine terrain offers adventurous intermediates and families a chance to explore beyond the usual groomer circuit. “Love Keystone and its low-key nature,” shared one fan. “Fun terrain, especially Bergman Bowl and the glades on The Outback.”

For families, Keystone has a lot to offer. Free parking, efficient lifts, a strong ski school, and a location just 90 minutes from Denver make the logistics easier, while base-area wagons help parents haul gear and tired kids. The village isn’t the most authentic, but it has what skiers need, plus fun-for-families extras such as character parades and seasonal events. Don’t miss the annual snow fort atop Dercum Mountain—it’s always a hit with younger skiers. “Keystone is the unquestionable gem of the I-70 corridor,” exclaimed one excited reader.

The resort also scores well for grooming, which is good news for skiers who like confidence-inspiring runs. But don’t assume the mountain is all mellow blues and beginner-friendly terrain. Stronger skiers can find challenging lines on North Peak plus glades in The Windows. Keystone may not rank among Colorado’s most demanding mountains, but those willing to venture beyond the frontside can find plenty to keep them interested. “There’s legit steep terrain here if you know where to look,” said a survey respondent.

Where Keystone falls short is local flavor. Its purpose-built village and convenient setup make for an easy vacation, but the atmosphere can feel more functional than distinctive compared with Colorado’s historic ski towns. Still, for families and Denver-area skiers who prize convenience, well-groomed runs, and straightforward logistics, Keystone remains a dependable choice.

“In a bad snow year (which this one was), Keystone’s snowmaking and grooming made it possible for them to outdistance everyone around them. This was the place to go all season. More than half of my total ski days were here this year.”

Keystone officially debuts Kindred Resort, its first premier luxury ski-in/ski-out hotel, at the base of the River Run Gondola. The new property brings upscale lodging and easy slope access to River Run Village.

Western spirit, family-friendly skiing, and a lively town make Steamboat a welcoming all-around getaway, even when the snow doesn’t cooperate.

Readers appreciate a resort that feels welcoming rather than intimidating, and Steamboat checks that box once again despite a small slip in the rankings. On the mountain, Steamboat offers a satisfying mix of groomers, tree skiing, and more adventurous terrain. Mahogany Ridge’s advanced and expert glades and bowls expand the options for stronger skiers, while the double-black glades Christmas Tree Bowl rewards those willing to venture beyond the cruisers. Still, challenge remains a weaker category in the survey, so experts seeking relentless steeps may want to temper their expectations.

For families and mixed-ability groups, though, the range of terrain—and the resort’s strong service culture—makes it easy to build a ski day that works for everyone. Steamboat scores high once again for its welcoming family vibe. The resort drives that point home with an enticing family-friendly perk offering free skiing for kids 12 and under from Nov. 21 through Dec. 15—no adult purchase required. “The resort really caters to families with young kids by offering some interesting areas for those kids to ski,” said one reader. “The ski school for young kids really leverages these areas, too.”

Steamboat’s other great asset is the town itself, but the much improved base village is beginning to give it a run for its money. The base has matured into a lively place to spend time after skiing, with upscale restaurants, an ice rink, casual slopeside bars, and a bit of nightlife that gives the resort a genuine après scene. But, downtown Steamboat Springs is still a huge draw. “Love the cool cowboy vibe downtown!” exclaimed one fan. It’s a place that retains its own identity, from Western art galleries to legendary F.M. Light & Sons, where you can shop for cowboy hats, boots, knickknacks and more. It’s this blend of mountain convenience and authentic character that keeps Steamboat feeling distinct from the more generic resort villages.

Parking remains a frustration, particularly during busy periods, though new policies aim to encourage carpools and make demand easier to manage. The resort’s popularity can also mean crowds, but recent lift and base-area improvements have helped skiers get moving more efficiently. It’s these types of skier-first initiatives that help Steamboat remain a compelling choice for visitors looking for a welcoming Colorado vacation with plenty of Western flavor.

“It’s not a ‘see and be seen’ kind of ski resort. You go here because you love to ski or you want your family to love to ski. You love the idea of the Wild, Wild West and you’d love to be riding a horse across a high mountain plain. You appreciate the simple things in life, and while this place is getting more popular, you’re hoping it always keeps its mountain-town feel.”

Steamboat is adding Barrow’s Bend, a new beginner-friendly green trail connecting Rendezvous Lodge to Sunshine Peak Lift, and honoring late local Olympian Moose Barrows. They’re raising the Maverick’s Halfpipe base, reducing the snow needed to build it by an estimated 40 to 60 percent and helping it open earlier. Advanced skiers and riders can also sign up for a new full-day Heli-Ready guided experience designed to build skills and confidence for heli-ski terrain.

Getting here is getting easier, too, thanks to air service expanding to 18 major U.S. airports, including new flights from Portland, Ore., and additional options from Austin and Houston.

Six peaks of varied skiing meet a lively historic town packed with great restaurants, après, nightlife, and classic Colorado character.

Breckenridge dropped 10 spots in this year’s rankings, a slide likely influenced by last winter’s disappointing snow across much of the West. But one lean season can’t erase what makes Breck such a reliable all-around ski vacation. Across six peaks, the resort serves up everything from cruisey groomers to steep, high-alpine terrain, with enough variety to keep a mixed-ability group happy for days. “Breckenridge has something for every type of skier,” said one reader. “Mellow greens for beginners and kids, plenty of intermediate terrain, and very challenging hike-to terrain.”

From a vacation perspective, one of Breck’s main draws is all it has going on off the slopes. The historic town has the kind of energy that makes a trip feel like a proper getaway, with a walkable Main Street lined with independent shops, excellent restaurants, lively bars, and live music venues. Readers gave the resort high marks for lodging, dining, nightlife, and après, reflecting a destination where there’s plenty to do after the last chair. “I love the apres-ski at the base of Peak 8 and Peak 7,” shared one survey respondent. “And there are so many restaurants on Main Street depending on your taste and budget.”

The drawbacks are familiar to anyone who has visited during peak periods. Weekend crowds can snarl the base areas, parking is expensive and sometimes inconvenient, and the overall cost of a Breck vacation can add up quickly. On-mountain dining also tends to feel pricey for what you get. Savvy skiers know to start early, move away from the busiest base areas, and explore beyond the most obvious runs. The resort’s size helps, but timing still matters.

For skiers who want a mountain with plenty of terrain and a town that stays lively long after the lifts close, Breckenridge remains a solid choice. Its ranking may have taken a hit after a challenging snow year, but the combination of varied skiing, comfortable lodging, standout dining, and a genuine ski-town atmosphere keeps it firmly in the conversation for a full-fledged Colorado getaway. “You really can’t beat the variety of terrain and the town of Breckenridge is so quaint!”

“While every ski area I’ve been to has its pros and cons, something about Breck always keeps me personally wanting to go back. I’ve been a handful of times now and still feel like there is still more terrain that is safely approachable even if it is slightly outside of my current skill level. And the town is the perfect place to spend a day off the slopes.”

Breckenridge is bringing back its historic “Kingdom of Breckenridge” identity for 2026–’27, reviving a name rooted in the town’s independent spirit. Look for enhanced customer-first initiatives such as new rental delivery options and updated on-mountain dining choices.

A welcoming, family-friendly mountain with well-groomed runs, genuinely helpful staff, and a refreshing value proposition.

Making its debut in SKI’s Resort Guide rankings, Tamarack Resort offers a different kind of destination experience: approachable, relaxed, and refreshingly down-to-earth. Set in Idaho’s West Central Mountains above Lake Cascade, Tamarack wins points for the things that can make or break a family ski trip, from friendly staff who go out of their way to help to well-groomed runs that make cruising the mountain a pleasure. It’s not trying to be the flashiest resort in the West, and that’s part of its charm. “Skiing the way it should be,” said one survey respondent. “No crowds, stress-free powder days, amazing food, the best top-to-bottom groomers, and incredible views.”

Tamarack’s strengths are especially apparent for families and recreational skiers. Grooming helps keep the skiing approachable, while the welcoming atmosphere makes it easy and less intimidating for everyone to find their footing. The resort also scored well for value, making it an ideal target destination for budget-minded skiers. Here, the experience feels less about luxury trappings and more about making skiing fun and accessible. “Tamarack is like having your own private mountain,” shared a reader. “ For a small resort, it gives you a lot of bang for your buck!”

The trade-off is that Tamarack’s terrain may not satisfy skiers looking for endless variety or expert-level challenges. Strong intermediates and families can find plenty to enjoy, but advanced skiers seeking steep, technical terrain may want a bigger mountain with more options. And while Tamarack has the essentials for a mountain getaway, its amenities are more simple and down-home compared to some of the pricier destination resorts on this list.

But for skiers who value a friendly welcome, dependable grooming, and a more affordable family ski vacation over luxury and high-adrenaline terrain, Tamarack makes a compelling case. Its first appearance in the rankings reflects a resort that knows what it does well: an approachable mountain experience where the people can be just as memorable as the skiing. “It’s a hidden gem. Don’t tell anyone!”

“Tamarack has been my secret go-to resort for over 20 years. The mountain is great and it’s never crowded. I am often the only person I can see on a run. And now that the amenities are coming online it’s even better.”

Tamarack is joining Ikon Pass as a bonus mountain this winter. Ikon Pass holders get two free days at the resort. On the slopes, skiers can take advantage of free guided tours with mountain hosts and a refreshed rental fleet with new standard and demo skis. Off the slopes, the resort is adding seasonal experiences and events, including full-moon yoga, snowshoe and wine walks, and a keep an eye out for the Miracle Bar pop-up this winter.

5000-plus acres of bowls, glades, and cruisers meet a lively European-style village with world-class dining and après—if you can stomach the crowds and prices.

Vail has been a fixture in our Top 30 for good reason: Few resorts deliver such an expansive menu of terrain alongside a full-fledged destination experience. The mountain slipped several spots this year, with last winter’s disappointing snow conditions likely playing a role, but its core appeal remains intact. Across 5,280 skiable acres, there are the legendary Back Bowls, technical glades, wide-open cruisers, and enough variety to keep different ability levels happy for days. You can spend a morning chasing powder stashes and an afternoon cruising long blues without ever feeling like you’ve skied the same run twice. “Nothing compares to the Back Bowls, Shangri-La Glade on a powder day, or ending the day on Riva Ridge,” said one longtime Vail skier.

Another strength is the resort’s pedestrian village, with its Bavarian-inspired architecture. It’s one of the liveliest in Colorado, packed with lodging options, restaurants, bars, and places to keep the day going long after last chair. Readers continue to reward Vail for its dining, lodging, and après scene, which help make it a true vacation destination. Recent lift upgrades have also helped move skiers around the sprawling resort more efficiently.

Of course, Vail’s popularity comes at a price—literally. Lift tickets, lodging, meals, and drinks can add up quickly, and the crowds remain a sore point, especially on weekends and holidays. Parking is another familiar headache. Weekday visits can offer a more relaxed experience, but anyone planning a peak-period trip should expect to share the mountain with plenty of other skiers. The snow also needs to cooperate. In a lean season like last winter, even Vail’s massive terrain can’t always deliver the experience its reputation promises, but consensus was that mountain ops did a commendable job with what they got: “Groomers on the frontside were very well maintained and skiable despite the conditions,” said one skier.

Still, Vail remains one of Colorado’s most complete ski vacations. The combination of big-mountain variety, comfortable places to stay, excellent dining, and a village with real energy is hard to beat. It may not be the best choice for budget-conscious skiers or those who prize solitude, but for visitors looking to pair serious skiing with a memorable resort experience, Vail continues to deliver.

“Vail is the pinnacle of Colorado skiing. The most and best variety of terrain. High-speed lifts exactly where they should be. Powder that sticks around for days. And some of the best bars, shops, and restaurants of any ski town.”

Vail is doubling down on off-slope entertainment this winter. Dobson Arena debuts as a reimagined 56,000-square-foot music venue in the heart of the village, and pop-up mountaintop performances at Eagle’s Nest and other locations are in the plans. The resort’s Après All Day series is doubling in size, with more than 50 artists scheduled to perform on weekends throughout the winter.

On the mountain, Epic Ascent adds a concierge and priority lift-line access to private ski lessons, and dining updates range from a rebuilt signature burger to the return of the Ice Bar at the entrance to the Back Bowls.

A high-alpine playground with 360-degree summit skiing, deep snow, and a delightfully adventurous vibe—without the destination-resort price tag.

After a long hiatus, Mt. Bachelor is back in our rankings, and it brings a distinctly Pacific Northwest flavor to the list. This 9,065-foot volcano in Oregon’s Central Cascades is a fickle beast: One minute the skies are clear, the next wind and fog turn the summit into a Middle Earth landscape. But that wild, weather-dependent personality is part of the appeal. When conditions cooperate, skiers can explore 360 degrees of terrain off the summit, with wide-open alpine runs, natural wind lips, and playful features that make every lap feel a little different. “You can always find less-crowded terrain,” said one reader. “The layout is easy to navigate.”

Bachelor’s 4,300-plus acres offer fast groomers, side-piste stashes,  hemlock forests, and adventurous above-treeline terrain. “On a good snow year you can ski anywhere off the top of the mountain,” said a survey respondent. “There’s really no place quite like it!” The mountain earns high marks for its lifts, too, helping skiers make the most of the sprawling layout. Snow is another major draw: With annual snowfall topping 450 inches, Bachelor can stack up deep midwinter conditions, making it a favorite for powder seekers and tree-skiing devotees alike.

The resort also scores well for value and parking, a welcome combination in an era when a ski day can feel like a logistical and financial undertaking. Bachelor’s laid-back atmosphere puts the emphasis on skiing rather than resort trappings, and the mountain’s scale means there’s plenty to explore without the crowds and complications of some better-known destinations. Still, the experience has its trade-offs. There’s no lodging at the base, and on-mountain amenities are limited, so visitors looking for a full-service village best look elsewhere.

Fortunately, nearby Bend offers a lively home base, with breweries, restaurants, and places to stay. For skiers who value big terrain, deep snow, efficient lifts, and a little adventure over luxury, Bachelor is a worthy addition to the rankings—and a reminder that sometimes the best days come with a bit of wildness.

“Big mountain with excellent lift system, good snow, and grooming. With the base at 6,000 feet it has a long season and rarely seems to lack snow. I have skied here many times and it rarely seems to be crowded during the week.”

Mt. Bachelor is upgrading its Northwest Express chairlift with rebuilt top and bottom terminals, a new electric motor and diesel backup, and buried power and fiber lines designed to improve reliability during storms.

A laid-back local favorite with deep snow, playful terrain, and wallet-friendly prices, Brighton keeps things refreshingly unpretentious.

Tucked into Big Cottonwood Canyon alongside Solitude, this community-minded mountain wins skiers over with its welcoming, no-frills vibe, reliable terrain, and prices that feel refreshingly reasonable by Wasatch standards. It may not have the name recognition or polish of some of its neighbors, but Brighton has a loyal following and a character all its own. “I never really went to this resort but headed there with the lack of snow elsewhere and was amazed by the quality of skiing,” said one reader. “Skied here for a week and will be back next year!”

The snow is a major draw. Brighton’s position in the Wasatch makes it a compelling option for powder seekers, with terrain that rewards everyone from casual cruisers to skiers looking to duck into the trees. “Brighton had some of the best snow in the Wasatch last year,” shared one survey respondent. And with value among its top-scoring categories, the resort offers a relatively affordable way to tap into Utah’s famously deep snow. For visitors who care more about fresh turns than fancy amenities, Brighton can feel like a well-kept secret, even if it’s hardly undiscovered.

Of course, easy access has its downsides. Brighton’s proximity to Salt Lake City makes it convenient for locals and visitors alike, but canyon traffic, parking headaches, and crowds can complicate a powder day. The base area is modest, with limited dining and après options and little in the way of nightlife. Readers also gave the resort lower marks for dining and guest service, underscoring that Brighton’s appeal lies more in the skiing than the extras.

Still, Brighton’s climb to No. 22 reflects the appeal of simplicity: good snow, fun terrain, a friendly atmosphere, and an appealing price point. It may not be for skiers who want a bustling village or a full slate of amenities, but for those who measure a great day by the turns they make, Brighton delivers.

“Brighton is a great local choice that has really evolved over the last few years thanks to increased investment and attention from Boyne. Expanded night riding, the Crest 6, and a new mid-mountain lodge make for a great experience.”

Brighton celebrates its 90th anniversary this winter and is expanding night skiing to six nights a week. There are also new ticket options including an Off-Peak Pass and a Flex Pass for three, four, or five days of skiing. On the mountain, the Milly Chalet has been revamped as a quick-service Mexican restaurant serving tacos and margaritas.

A fiercely independent spirit, Southwestern soul, and some of the continent’s most challenging in-bounds terrain make Taos a mountain skiers fall hard for.

Taos climbed two spots this year despite the fact that last winter’s lean snow season hit the Southwest particularly hard—and that’s saying something. The Reader Resort Survey still shows what makes Taos special: a true sense of character, terrain that demands respect, and skiers who are eager to return year after year. Taos has an old-school spirit and a spicy Southwestern personality that’s unique to ski country.

Taos scored among its best in the challenge category, thanks to marquee steeps on Kachina Peak and hike-to terrain in West Basin. “I have skied here for over 50 years and am still discovering new lines and runs,” admitted one longtime skier. Yet Taos isn’t exclusively for experts. Its 1,294 acres are manageable enough for families to explore together, while traditional European-style Ski Weeks and the slopeside Blake Hotel lend the resort a distinctly alpine feel—with a New Mexico twist.

Taos also scored well for parking, an unsexy but practical perk that can make a ski day feel easier. The trade-off is a relatively small base village, with limited lodging and restaurant options compared with larger destinations. Après and grooming aren’t its strong suits, either. For a fuller taste of the region, make time for the town of Taos, where galleries, chile-forward cuisine, and the historic Taos Pueblo—a UNESCO World Heritage Site—offer plenty of reasons to stay off the mountain for a while. “Lots to do once you’re off the slopes and the New Mexico food is to die for!” said one survey respondent.

For skiers who value personality over polish, Taos has a way of getting under your skin. Its combination of serious terrain, independent character, and skier loyalty suggests that Taos’ devotees are in it for the long haul. When the snow cooperates, this mountain’s mix of steep lines, high-desert scenery, and Southwestern flavor is tough to replicate.

“Taos Ski Valley has kept its original charm. Definitely no corporate vibe here. When the snow is good, it’s a wonderful place.”

Taos has invested heavily in mountain improvements for 2026–’27, including additional glading, early-season snowmaking capabilities, and a satellite-based snow-depth mapping system to help crews groom more efficiently.

Big-mountain terrain, steep lines, and a spectacular Lake Tahoe backdrop make this a must-ski for experts willing to brave the crowds.

Palisades Tahoe is back in the rankings, and it’s easy to see why. Year after year, the resort earns high marks for challenge and terrain variety, two categories that matter most to skiers who like their mountains steep, technical, and a little intimidating.
